chapters.title: 1. Exam Prep and How to Use This Guide

blocks.text: This guide covers every module of the APEA 2026 FNP/AGPCNP Review manual (22 chapters, 59 PDF parts), in manual order. Each chapter keeps the manual's tables, criteria, doses and practice questions; answers to practice questions are collected in the answer key at the end. Sections 18 (Pediatrics) and 19 (Growth & Development) are FNP-only. Answers marked † in the key had more than one defensible choice.

sections.title: AANP vs ANCC — choose one, not both

blocks.text: Consider question format, cost (student membership), and recertification. Both confer board certification.
Review the exam blueprint and reference list for the exam you choose.
ANCC divides planning and implementation; check the ANCC blueprint for its percentages.
ANCC does not publish content-area percentages. On the AANP FNP exam, 78% of items are adult (young, middle, older).

items: Assessment: subjective data (HPI, ROS, PMH), objective data (physical exam), ordering, performing and interpreting diagnostic and screening tests.
Diagnosis: formulate and prioritize differentials, recognize urgent and emergent conditions, establish a confirmatory diagnosis.
Planning: patient-centered plan, immediate referrals and consultations, pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic therapy, education, counseling and health promotion.
Evaluation: effectiveness of the plan, barriers to care, modifying the plan, additional referral, monitoring ongoing response.
Complete the entire review course; note areas of discomfort; answer the 200 course questions.
Use reliable resources until every question is answered: Clinical Practice Guidelines (5th ed.), USPSTF, IDSA, ADA, AHA, ACOG, CDC, NIH. When guidelines disagree, find the common ground.
Take a predictor exam: it simulates the exam, predicts pass likelihood, identifies gaps, and sets a timeline.
Plot the study plan on a calendar. Length depends on the content areas to cover, but no longer than 3 months.

blocks.text: For weak areas (example: Men's Health): focus on clinical guidelines; know when to refer, prescribe and monitor; review diagnostic criteria and normal vs abnormal; use teach-back; make mind maps or flash cards.

Exam day: take a 1–2 minute break every hour. Never assume information not given — everything needed is provided. Use the technique. Answer ALL questions. Don't expect to know everything. Breathe.

items: Stewardship prevents overuse, misuse and abuse, minimizes resistance, reduces cost. The 5 Ds: Drug (right drug, right bug), Dosing (optimal), Drug route, Duration (suitable), De-escalation (timely to pathogen-directed therapy). Susceptibility does not equal sensitivity, due to resistance.

Duration: most indications 5–7 days; expect clinical improvement at 48 hours. Longer: strep pharyngitis 10 days, pyelonephritis 14 days, severe infections, immunocompromised patients, many pediatric indications.
Empiric therapy = first-line drug targeting the most likely organisms. Weigh risk of morbidity/mortality (higher risk → broader spectrum), side-effect risk, contraindications, the local antibiogram.

Culture when: patient cannot afford treatment failure; severe infection; risk of complications; unsure of organism or whether infection is present; failed empiric treatment; high resistance risk (recent antibiotics). The site/sample must be appropriate.

sections.title: The beta-lactam ring: allergy and resistance

blocks.text: Penicillins and cephalosporins share the beta-lactam ring. It matters for allergy (cross-reactivity) and for resistance (beta-lactamase destroys the ring). IgE cross-reactivity is very uncommon; it is most likely when the R1 side chain is similar: 1–8% with 1st/2nd-generation cephalosporins, <1% with 3rd-generation. Fewer than 1% of people have a true PCN allergy.

items: Rule 1 — NEVER give a 1st-generation cephalosporin if the PCN reaction was anaphylaxis or hives. IgE-mediated type I reactions worsen with each exposure. Other IgE signs: hypotension, laryngeal edema, wheezing, angioedema, urticaria.
Rule 2 — Cautious use of 2nd/3rd-generation cephalosporins after a type I reaction. Dissimilar side chains mean less cross-reactivity; less still if >10 years since the reaction.
Rule 3 — Any cephalosporin may be given if the PCN reaction was a morbilliform rash (maculopapular drug eruption, T-cell mediated, type IV).

Chronic inflammation causes structural change and persistent, progressive airflow obstruction. Airway abnormalities → chronic bronchitis; alveolar abnormalities → emphysema. Symptoms: progressive dyspnea, chronic cough, recurrent respiratory infections.

Risk factors — GET: Genes (alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, rare) · Environment (smoking/exposure, vaping, cannabis, air pollution, indoor stoves, animal dung, crop residues, chemicals) · Time / lung-function trajectory (prematurity, low birth weight, gestational smoking, severe childhood infections, poverty/low SES).

blocks.text: ICS criteria: eosinophils ≥300/µL, exacerbation requiring hospitalization, or asthma.

Exacerbation: ↑ dyspnea and/or cough and sputum worsening over <14 days, ± tachypnea, tachycardia. Triggers: viruses (influenza, rhinovirus), bacteria (H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, S. pneumoniae), pollutants, excessive heat. Rule out pneumonia, PE, HF.

Management (mild–moderate, outpatient): SABA (may combine with SAMA; spacer or nebulizer); continue long-acting bronchodilators; prednisone 40 mg/day × 5 days; antibiotics for increased sputum purulence or high risk (≥65, comorbidities). Admit: severe symptoms; respiratory distress or SaO2 <92% or >3% below baseline; new cyanosis or AMS; failed initial treatment; serious comorbidities (HF, DM, arrhythmia); insufficient home support.

Triggered airway hyperresponsiveness and inflammation: wheezing, cough, SOB, chest tightness. History: episodic and night symptoms; personal/family asthma, allergies, atopy. Triggers: exercise, respiratory infections, inhaled allergens (dust/chemicals, pet dander, cockroach droppings, mold, occupational), air irritants (pollution, smoke, cold air, odors).

Diagnosis (age >5): typical symptoms with supportive H&P. Spirometry available → reversible airflow limitation, FEV1 or FVC ↑ ≥12–15% → treat. Not available → rule out differentials, treat empirically, re-evaluate in 1–3 months.

sections.title: Lung cancer screening and smoking cessation

blocks.text: Screen generally healthy adults 50–80 with a 20 pack-year history who currently smoke or quit within 15 years (USPSTF; ACS: ever smoked). Screening = secondary prevention; test = low-dose CT, annually.

Smoking cessation: motivational interviewing; assess readiness at every visit and tailor to it. Set a quit date ~2 weeks out. Varenicline, bupropion and combination long-/short-acting NRT are equally effective. Behavioral tips: avoid triggers; 5-minute delay when cravings hit.
Q1. Healthy adult with acute bronchitis — next step? (1) Ciprofloxacin (2) PA/lateral CXR (3) Prednisone injection (4) Rest and fluids.
Q2. Best test to screen for influenza has: (1) high sensitivity (2) low sensitivity (3) high specificity (4) low specificity.
Q3. Expected CXR finding, 67-year-old with pneumonia: (1) pulmonary congestion (2) cavitating opacities (3) lobar infiltrates (4) hilar enlargement.
Q4. Healthy 58-year-old with CAP — first-line? (1) Doxycycline 100 mg BID (2) Azithromycin 500 mg then 250 mg ×4 days (3) Amoxicillin 500 mg TID (4) Amoxicillin 1,000 mg TID.
Q5. Healthy 52-year-old, PCN allergy (hives), resistance rates unknown: (1) doxycycline 100 mg BID (2) levofloxacin 750 mg daily (3) cefpodoxime 200 mg BID (4) azithromycin.

Q9. Statement needing more education: (1) COPD is progressive (2) goal is symptoms and QOL (3) quitting smoking will keep COPD symptoms from getting worse (4) avoiding infections slows progression.
Q10. New COPD, GOLD A — best regimen for daily symptoms: (1) fluticasone + levalbuterol (2) PRN prednisone (3) tiotropium daily + albuterol PRN (4) salmeterol BID.

Q11–12. New COPD, walks slower than peers on level ground, has SABA PRN — group and prescription: (1) ipratropium/albuterol (2) ipratropium + tiotropium (3) umeclidinium/vilanterol (4) fluticasone/umeclidinium/vilanterol.
Q13. 27-year-old using albuterol 2–3×/week — MART regimen: (1) add salmeterol (2) add formoterol (3) stop albuterol, add formoterol/budesonide BID and PRN (4) add tiotropium.

blocks.text: Anemia is a reduction in at least one RBC measure — RBC count, hemoglobin, or hematocrit — and is never normal. Exam checklist: IDA, thalassemia, anemia of chronic disease, G6PD deficiency, B12/folate deficiency, thrombocytopenia, CBC differential interpretation.
"Normal doesn't always mean normal": a perimenopausal patient whose Hgb falls from 14.6 to 12.5 g/dL after a heavy cycle (normal 12.1–15.2) with SOB and fatigue has a real problem.

items: Reticulocytes (immature RBCs): normal 0–2.5% in adults; reflect marrow production. Anemia should raise the count; anemia with a low retic count means the marrow isn't responding.
RDW (variation in RBC size): <15% normal, >15% abnormal.
Iron panel: serum iron = circulating; ferritin = storage; TIBC = capacity to bind/move iron. Egg-carton analogy: high iron → low TIBC; low iron → high TIBC.
Peripheral smear: a visual description of the cells; consider for any anemia.

blocks.text: Common: iron deficiency, thalassemia. Less common: anemia of chronic disease (<20%), sideroblastic anemia, lead toxicity (presents just like IDA).
Iron-deficiency anemia — microcytic, hypochromic. Causes: blood loss (most common, GYN or GI); low intake, poor absorption, pregnancy. Usually asymptomatic until Hgb ≤10.

rows: Fatigue, weakness, headache, irritability, exercise intolerance

blocks.text: Iron-rich foods: liver, lentils, spinach, clams/oysters, red beans, rice, fortified grains.
Elemental iron: old recommendation 150–200 mg daily; new recommendation 15–20 mg daily.

Thalassemia — genetic abnormality of hemoglobin formation → abnormal RBCs, hemolysis or impaired erythropoiesis. Microcytic, hypochromic; target cells on smear. Diagnostic test: hemoglobin electrophoresis.

Anemia of chronic disease (chronic inflammation) — RBC lifespan 60–90 days (normal 100–120). Normocytic, normochromic (long-standing may become microcytic, hypochromic). Causes: RA, morbid obesity, colon cancer, uncontrolled DM, CHF, COPD, CKD, autoimmune disease, chronic infection (HIV). Take a good history; manage by controlling the underlying condition.

B12 (cobalamin) and folate (B9) together form RBCs, WBCs and platelets and are needed for DNA/RNA; deficiency of either causes megaloblastic anemia. Usually asymptomatic; severe B12 deficiency gives unexplained neurologic symptoms — cognitive changes, neuropathy, glossitis.

Platelets <150,000; petechiae, purpura and bleeding are far more likely below 50,000. A patient presenting only with a petechial rash needs a CBC.

blocks.text: Covers vertigo, head trauma, concussion, Bell's palsy, headaches, neuropathy, tremors, dementia/delirium and cranial nerves. For each: presentation, diagnosis, differentials, management, follow-up and when to refer.

Sensation of spinning, movement or disequilibrium with many etiologies — get a thorough history. Peripheral = vestibular system/inner ear (BPPV, otitis media, Ménière). Central = brainstem or cerebellum (stroke, MS, brain tumor, meningitis).
Workup: full neuro exam; Dix–Hallpike (canalithiasis of the posterior semicircular canal = BPPV); HINTS (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew — abnormal suggests central).

blocks.text: BPPV is managed in primary care: Epley repositioning; first-generation antihistamine — best evidence meclizine (Antivert) 25–100 mg, reserved for highly disruptive symptoms (watch anticholinergic effects); antinausea meds. Refer for everything except BPPV.

blocks.text: Concussion (mild acute TBI): progressive improvement within 7–10 days; resolution by 1 month; may need school/work accommodations. Symptoms: emotional lability/irritability, headache, dizziness, abnormal balance, mental fogginess, concentration/memory deficits, sleep changes. Refer for neurologic decompensation.

CN VII palsy: idiopathic, acute, spontaneous facial paralysis; clinical diagnosis. House–Brackmann grades I (normal) to VI (complete paralysis). Findings: forehead flattening, drooping, loss of nasolabial fold, poor eyelid closure, altered tearing (dry or spilling), otalgia, taste disturbance, tingling/numbness.

blocks.text: Course: peak 1–2 days → stable ~3 weeks → improving 2–3 months → recovery 3–6 months. Prevent complications: corneal abrasion and psychological distress.
Primary (overactivity of pain-sensing structures): migraine, tension, cluster. Secondary (underlying pathology, often red flags): sinusitis, medication overuse, hypertension, stroke.

SNOOP-10 red flags: S systemic symptoms, secondary risk factors · N neurologic symptoms (AMS) · O onset abrupt (thunderclap) · O older (new or progressive >50) · P pattern change, papilledema, positional, precipitated by Valsalva, progressive, pregnancy, posttraumatic, painful eye, pathology of immune system, painkiller use · 10 10/10 severity. Papilledema = optic disc swelling from ↑ICP; almost always bilateral.

blocks.text: Migraine without aura (ICHD-3): 4–72 h; ≥2 of unilateral, pulsating, moderate–severe, aggravated by routine activity; ≥1 of N/V, photophobia or phonophobia; ≥5 attacks (<5 = "probable migraine"); no other cause. With aura: ~25% of migraineurs; meets migraine criteria with ≥2 aura attacks; fully reversible visual, sensory, motor, brainstem, retinal or speech changes developing over 5–60 min before the headache. Risk factors: female, age 30–39, genetics. Triggers: stress, hormones, fasting, weather, sleep disruption, food or drink.

rows: Watch CIs/AEs; more effective combined with triptans
Suma-, zolmi-, nara-, riza-, almo-, ele-, frovatriptan
CI: basilar migraine, ischemic stroke, MI, Prinzmetal angina, uncontrolled HTN

Not vasoconstrictive; may reduce N/V; not first-line

blocks.text: Medication overuse headache (ICHD-3): preexisting headache disorder; headache ≥15 days/month; regular overuse >3 months — >10 days/month of ergotamines, triptans, opioids or combination analgesics, or >15 days/month of simple analgesics; no better explanation. All of these classes can cause it. Management: withdraw the overused drug; start prophylaxis.

Prophylaxis indications: >4 attacks/month or >12 h per attack; significant disability; risk of MOH; abortives ineffective, contraindicated or poorly tolerated; menstrual migraine. 3–6 month trial; start low, titrate.

blocks.text: Risk factors: HTN, hyperlipidemia, obesity, DM; depression and isolation; cognitive and physical inactivity; smoking, alcohol; hearing loss; head injury; age.

Workup: history from patient and significant other; MoCA (≥94% sensitivity, ≤60% specificity, free, multilingual) or MMSE (not free); labs to rule out look-alikes (CBC, B12, TSH); biomarkers (CSF, serum, PET) still research; refer if unclear or atypical. Always screen for depression (PHQ-2: little interest in doing things? feeling down, depressed, hopeless?).

Presumptive Alzheimer: impairment in >1 domain; significant insidious decline; impairs ADLs; delirium and other mental disorders excluded. Domains: learning and memory, language, executive function, complex attention, perceptual-motor, social cognition. Agreement between history and mental exam = probable AD.

rows: Donepezil (Aricept, ODT), rivastigmine (Exelon patch), galantamine (Razadyne IR/ER)

blocks.text: Some patients meet criteria for monoclonal antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab).

Management: safety first (alerts, door locks, locked medication cabinets); minimize anxiety (distract and redirect, routine, calm reassurance). Neuropsychiatric symptoms: assess other causes; nonpharmacologic first; depression → SSRI/SNRI; delusions/hallucinations/agitation → brexpiprazole (Rexulti) or off-label olanzapine, quetiapine; sleep → melatonin, suvorexant (Belsomra).

Delirium = sudden, significant change in brain function. Causes: drugs (medication change, substances); medical (AFib, electrolytes, dehydration, nutrition); infection (UTI, pneumonia); brain insults (head injury, CNS infection); environment (hospitalization, sensory deprivation).

blocks.text: Q1. Finding suggesting central vertigo: (1) nystagmus stops with fixation (2) hearing impairment (3) normal neuro exam (4) unable to maintain balance walking.
Q2. Positive Dix–Hallpike: (1) dizziness resolves immediately (2) doll's-eye reflex (3) nystagmus <60 seconds (4) vomits on the NP's shoes. Likely diagnosis?
Q3. 65-year-old fell and hit head 2 h ago — refer for CT if: (1) GCS 15 (2) vomited once (3) forehead laceration (4) age 65.

Q4. 12-year-old, mild concussion, normal neuro exam — return to full activity: (1) after 48 h rest (2) when tolerating a full school day (3) when headache resolves (4) after a 6-day return-to-play protocol without recurrent symptoms.
Q5. Sudden unilateral facial droop, can't raise right eyebrow or blink, present on waking: (1) Lyme (2) Bell's palsy (3) stroke (4) tumor.
Q6. Headache feature needing imaging: (1) explosive eye pain resolving in 1 h (2) severe headache on dabigatran (3) N/V (4) visual distortion before headache.
Q7. True about triptans: (1) if one fails, switch class (2) limit to 2 days/month (3) sumatriptan SQ is recommended for cluster headache (4) never with an NSAID.
Q8. Drug classes causing medication overuse headache: (1) opioids (2) triptans (3) simple analgesics (4) all of the above.

Q9. True of diabetic neuropathy: (1) duration and severity of hyperglycemia are primary risk factors (2) begins unilaterally (3) reversible with glucose control (4) weekly foot inspection prevents amputation.
Q10. 62-year-old new hand tremor — essential tremor if it: (1) starts unilaterally, pill-rolling (2) most apparent with hand supported (3) with bradykinesia (4) at the end of goal-directed movement.

Q11. Match each tremor to its likely diagnosis: unilateral foot tremor at rest; symmetric voice and head tremor; induced by valproic acid; managed with primidone or propranolol; with bradykinesia and rigidity; with anxiety, heat intolerance and fatigue.

Q12. Family member reports an older patient's cognitive decline — true: (1) examine without family input (2) patient is always aware of impairment (3) complete a thorough medication review (4) determine whether the family member has medical POA.
Q13. 70-year-old with 3 months of progressive memory change — least likely: (1) B12 deficiency (2) depression (3) syphilis (4) delirium.

blocks.text: Covers depression, bipolar screening, suicidality, anxiety, PTSD, substance use, adult ADHD and insomnia. Know presentation, screenings, criteria, differentials, management, course, follow-up and when to refer.

Mood is shaped by biology (neurotransmitters, hormones), psychology, physiologic state and environment. Stimuli: fatigue, hunger, stress, fear, anger, genetics, toxins; the postsynaptic impulse is excitatory or inhibitory.

rows: Appetite, mood, anxiety, sleep, sex drive
Energy, reward, motivation, mood, attention, executive function
Calm and relaxation; anxiety and sleep

blocks.text: The most common mental health disorder; 50% go undiagnosed because the right questions aren't asked. Ask: "Within the last 2 weeks, have you experienced…" SIG-E-CAPS: Sleep · Interest (anhedonia) · Guilt (worthlessness) · Energy · Concentration · Appetite · Psychomotor agitation · Suicidality.

All have similar sensitivity and specificity. History: prior episodes and treatment; family history (30–40% genetic); stressors, social, occupation (60–70% situational); psychiatric comorbidities that confound (bipolar, anxiety, alcohol/drug use); medical comorbidities that complicate (DM, HF, dementia, COPD).

DSM-5-TR MDD: symptoms ≥2 weeks; anhedonia or depressed mood must be present; ≥5 symptoms most of the day nearly every day; distress; no other cause; no mania/hypomania. "Other specified depressive disorder" = clinically significant but below MDD criteria.

Labs — consider secondary causes in older patients, first episode, severe onset, or no clear precipitant: standard CBC, CMP, TSH; older adults FBG, B12, folate; impaired nutrition B12, folate; fertile females pregnancy test; suspected substance use urine drug screen.

rows: Offer treatment; clinical judgment and shared decision-making
Active treatment: psychotherapy, medication or both

blocks.text: Treatment: shared decision-making; depression-focused psychotherapy/CBT; generally a second-generation antidepressant (SSRI or SNRI); bupropion (NDRI) and serotonin modulators also effective.

rows: Lower dose, add bupropion, switch to non-serotonergic drug or fluvoxamine

blocks.text: Pregnancy: generally safe; escitalopram or sertraline preferred; avoid paroxetine; discuss risks/benefits. Lactation: low levels in milk; continue the pregnancy SSRI. Weigh risks of untreated depression.
Exclude bipolar disorder before an SSRI. Major depression may be its presenting symptom. Screen with the Mood Disorder Questionnaire (15 items; sensitivity 58%, specificity 93%).

rows: Excess energy, grandiosity, fast speech, distractibility, agitation, hallucinations, impulsivity; substance misuse, legal and relationship problems common
Like mania but not severe enough to impair function; productive goal-directed activity, creativity, inflated self-esteem

blocks.text: Bipolar I: ≥1 manic episode (major depression less likely). Bipolar II: ≥1 hypomanic episode, ≥1 major depressive episode, no mania. If suspected: do NOT start antidepressants — refer.
Dosing: start low, go slow, don't stop, be patient (sertraline usual 50–200 mg; older adult start 25 mg).
First episode: continue ≥6 months after remission.

rows: MDD, GAD, fibromyalgia, neuropathy, chronic MSK pain; least likely to raise BP
MDD, social anxiety, cataplexy; caution with bleeding risk

blocks.text: SNRI side effects: nausea, dizziness, diaphoresis, ↑BP (except duloxetine), sexual dysfunction, bleeding, hyponatremia.

Bupropion (NDRI, Wellbutrin): MDD, seasonal affective disorder, smoking cessation (Zyban), ADHD (off-label); with naltrexone (Contrave) for weight loss. CI: seizures, uncontrolled HTN. Monitor BP. AEs: dry mouth, nausea, insomnia, anxiety. No sexual side effects or weight gain; less withdrawal.

Discontinuation syndrome — likely if stopped abruptly, tapered over only 2–7 days, switched to a drug with different PK, 3–4 doses skipped, or brand switched to generic. Symptoms: fatigue, headache, nausea, agitation/anxiety, dizziness, insomnia, flu-like illness (chills without fever, myalgias). Taper over 2–4 weeks if on an SSRI ≥6 weeks.

rows: Taper old while increasing new, 1–2 weeks

blocks.text: Serotonin syndrome (serotonin toxicity): from combining serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, St. John's wort, dextromethorphan, tramadol, TCAs, cyclobenzaprine). ↑BP, HR, temperature; confusion, restlessness, agitation; headache, muscle rigidity, N/V, tremor, shivering; high mortality.

All antidepressants carry an FDA boxed warning for increased suicidality, reported most in ages 18–24, at initiation and in the first 1–2 months. Efficacy studies: no change in suicide deaths; starting an antidepressant does not cause new-onset ideation; SSRIs reduce ideation. Weigh risks and benefits and put supports in place.

Risk factors: psychiatric disorder, hopelessness, impulsivity, isolation, prior attempts, family history, substance use, prolonged stress, abuse/neglect/trauma. Highest risk: never married; male (4:1); age 75+; firearms are the most common method. 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. Actively suicidal with a plan → activate EMS.
Anxiety becomes pathologic when its intensity is disproportionate to the trigger.

rows: Paroxysmal, minutes to an hour; worry about future attacks

blocks.text: GAD (DSM-5-TR): excessive worry more days than not for ≥6 months; significant distress/impairment; ≥3 of: restlessness, muscle tension, irritability, impaired concentration, easy fatigue, sleep disturbance; not due to substances or another diagnosis.

GAD management: shared decision-making by severity and impact; CBT or psychotherapy. First-line SSRIs and SNRIs. Short-term PRN bridge by patient characteristics: benzodiazepines or hydroxyzine (nonaddictive). Adjunct: buspirone (add-on to SSRI/SNRI, daily dosing), exercise, smoking cessation.
Marked cognitive, affective and/or behavioral disruption in response to trauma.

Irritability/aggression, reckless behavior, on edge, sleep disturbance, hypervigilance; began after the event

blocks.text: First-line: trauma-focused psychotherapy; refer for psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy as indicated.

Substances (by social acceptability): caffeine, tobacco/nicotine, alcohol, prescription drugs (opioids, stimulants, gabapentin), marijuana, illicit drugs (cocaine, heroin, hallucinogens, inhalants). Assess: ever used, pattern, last use, frequency; consequences (job loss, divorce, jail); patient's perception; readiness to change.

rows: "How many times in the past year have you had 5 (men) / 4 (women) or more drinks in a day?"

Severity: mild 2–3, moderate 4–5, severe ≥6. Understand the MAT Act; consider referral.

blocks.text: Combined presentation = both. Rating scales: Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (WHO), Conners' Adult ADHD Rating Scale, Wender Utah. Assess comorbidities, substance use, age of onset.
DSM-5 (children and adults): symptoms before age 12; >6 months; in ≥2 settings; interfere with functioning. <17 years: 6 symptoms per domain; ≥17 years: ≥5.

Management: CBT + medication preferred. First-line stimulants — amphetamines (Adderall), methylphenidate (Ritalin). Common AEs: weight loss, headache, insomnia, dry mouth, irritability, dysphoria; rare: priapism, ↑BP, tics. Alternatives: atomoxetine (Strattera), viloxazine (Qelbree); bupropion off-label. Active substance use disorder contraindicates stimulants. Refer for comorbid psychological disorders (ODD, emotional problems) or neurologic/medical disorders (tics, autism, sleep disorders), unclear diagnosis, or poor response.

Always consult the Beers Criteria for older adults. OTC aids: antihistamines (diphenhydramine, doxylamine) block histamine receptors; melatonin regulates the sleep–wake cycle; herbals (valerian, chamomile, lavender) may calm.

blocks.text: Acute: gallbladder inflammation, usually gallstones (acalculous 5–10%). Steady, severe RUQ pain, sometimes colicky, epigastric or radiating to the right shoulder; triggered by a high-fat meal; fever; worse with movement. Murphy's sign = inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation. Preferred imaging: abdominal ultrasound.

Chronic (gallbladder dyskinesia, biliary colic): smoldering course alternating with acute colic; may lead to acute cholecystitis. Risk factors: female, obesity, pregnancy, advancing age. Imaging: ultrasound; cholescintigraphy (HIDA).

Retrograde flow of gastric contents into the esophagus: poor esophageal motility, dysfunctional LES, increased gastric volume and pressure. Reflux can be physiologic or pathologic. Presumptive diagnosis: pathologic symptoms ≥2 days/week without alarm features. Treatment: weight loss if appropriate, dietary modification, PPIs first-line.
Alarm symptoms — REFER: new onset at ≥60; GI bleeding or new IDA; anorexia/weight loss; dysphagia/odynophagia; vomiting (obstruction); GI cancer in a first-degree relative.
No relief after 8 weeks of a PPI → refer. Resolved after 8 weeks → stop and see whether symptoms recur in 2–4 weeks.

Barrett's esophagus — esophageal dysplasia from chronic GERD. Risk factors: male; age ≥50; non-Hispanic White; GERD ≥5–10 years; smoking; hiatal hernia; Barrett's or esophageal cancer in a first-degree relative.

Diverticulosis = sac-like protrusions of the bowel wall; 70–80% asymptomatic. Complications: diverticular bleeding (5–15%), diverticulitis (4–15%), abscess, fistula, obstruction, perforation. Classic diverticulitis: LLQ pain, nausea, low-grade fever, low-fiber diet; confirm with CT.

ACP 2021 outpatient management: antibiotics selectively, not routinely; pain control; liquid diet advanced as tolerated over 2–3 days; no repeat imaging if improving; colonoscopy in 6–8 weeks if none in the past year.

blocks.text: Complicated UTI: individualized, 7–14 days. Treat promptly. Phenazopyridine: no more than 2 days; discolors urine. Prevention: cranberry products, hydration, void every 2–4 hours and after intercourse, topical estrogen if postmenopausal. Hematuria requires further evaluation.

Urine culture: recurrent/refractory infection, risk of complications, catheter, complicated UTI, suspected multidrug resistance, uncertain diagnosis. Positive: >100,000 organisms midstream; >1,000 by catheterization.

Infection of the upper tract and renal parenchyma. UTI symptoms plus fever, chills, malaise; flank, pelvic or perineal pain; CVA, abdominal or suprapubic tenderness; may look ill. UA: pyuria, bacteriuria, hematuria, mild proteinuria, WBC casts; CBC leukocytosis.

Outpatient if clinically stable and tolerating PO; collect culture before antibiotics. First-line: levofloxacin daily ×5 days; ciprofloxacin q12h ×7 days; TMP-SMX DS q12h ×7–14 days. Alternatives: ceftriaxone 1 g IM ×1 PLUS amox/clav PO q12h ×14 days, or an oral 3rd/4th-generation cephalosporin.

Prevalence 25–40%; 40% of women >70; <30% of incontinent women seek care. Types: stress (↑abdominal pressure, weak pelvic floor), urge (involuntary bladder contraction), overflow (urethral blockage), neurogenic (disturbed nerve function).

Behavioral management first-line: bladder training; fluids (minimize after dinner; diuretics in the afternoon, not at night); pelvic floor exercises (Kegel, yoga, pelvic tilts). Nonpharmacologic: biofeedback, nerve stimulation, pessary (prolapse), surgery and weight loss (stress).

Urge/mixed pharmacotherapy: anticholinergics first-line — oxybutynin (Ditropan), tolterodine (Detrol); dry mouth, dry eyes, GI effects ("can't see, pee, spit, …"). Alternative: mirabegron (Myrbetriq), beta-3 agonist, fewer side effects. Postmenopausal: topical estrogen.

5 Ps: partners, practices, protection, past STIs, pregnancy intention. High risk: unprotected sex, multiple partners, sex under the influence, early initiation, high-risk partner. Patients are often asymptomatic; females: discharge, dysuria, salpingitis, abnormal bleeding, pelvic pain; males: dysuria, penile discharge, pelvic pain. Test and treat to minimize complications.

HSV-1 and HSV-2 both cause genital herpes; HSV-2 causes most recurrences and raises HIV risk 2–3-fold; genital HSV-1 rarely recurs. Exposure is ubiquitous. Primary = no HSV antibodies; first outbreak, may be severe and prolonged. Nonprimary = preexisting antibodies; recurrences common, less severe, asymptomatic shedding (most in the first year of HSV-2).

Testing: genital lesion → NAAT (most accurate) or culture. Consider serology if symptoms could be herpes, partner has genital herpes, or signs need confirmation. Exposed to HSV-2 with negative IgG → repeat in 12 weeks.

CDC screening: average risk = one-time between 13 and 64; high risk = at least annually (MSM; partner with HIV; >1 partner since last test; shared injection equipment; sex for drugs or money; another STI; hepatitis or TB; sex with anyone in these groups).

Reduces transmission by >99%. Educate all sexually active patients; identify high-risk patients. Eligibility: high risk; nonreactive HIV Ag/Ab; no possible exposure in the prior 4 weeks; no signs of acute HIV; proper workup and recurring diagnostics.

Murmurs are sounds of turbulent flow through the great vessels or across a valve; two valves (mitral and aortic) cause nearly all adult trouble. Stenotic valves don't OPEN properly; regurgitant valves don't CLOSE properly.

WHERE — aortic RSB 2nd ICS; pulmonic LSB 2nd ICS; tricuspid lower left sternum 4th–5th ICS; mitral apex, 5th ICS left midclavicular line. blocks.text: First medication: metformin usually — effective (↓A1c 1–2%), inexpensive, reduces CV risk, well tolerated, weight neutral. GLP-1, GLP-1/GIP or SGLT-2 can be first-line with obesity, high ASCVD risk or CKD. Avoid metformin with reduced eGFR (e.g., 42 — don't start <45).

Add 4 units rapid-acting (or 10% of basal) with the largest meal; consider decreasing basal by 4 units or 10%. Increase mealtime insulin 1–2 units twice weekly until postprandial glucose is at target.

blocks.text: Functional problems: hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism (primary, subclinical, secondary). Structural problems: goiter (enlargement), thyroiditis (inflammation), nodules (benign, toxic, cancer). Structural problems can cause functional problems.

items: TSH (anterior pituitary) stimulates thyroid hormone production. It is the most sensitive measure of thyroid function — the "early warning system": it changes before T3/T4, is more reliable, and a small change in T3/T4 produces a large change in TSH. Used to screen and to monitor replacement.
T4 (thyroxine): 4 iodine atoms, 80% released by thyroid; free T4 is active (99.5% bound/inactive); more specific to hypothyroidism.
T3 (triiodothyronine): 3 iodine atoms; 20% from thyroid, most converted from T4 peripherally; more specific to hyperthyroidism.
Negative feedback: ↓T3/T4 → hypothalamus TRH → anterior pituitary TSH → thyroid T3/T4 → levels restored.

blocks.text: Primary = problem in the thyroid (e.g., autoimmune). Secondary = originates outside the thyroid; may involve other hormones; feedback-loop failure (refer).

Subclinical hypothyroidism (↑TSH, normal FT4): TSH >10 → treat to prevent progression (25–50 mcg or 1.6 mcg/kg/day IBW). TSH <10 → treatment usually not beneficial; recheck in 6–12 months or if symptoms increase.
Primary hypothyroidism (>95%): usually Hashimoto thyroiditis (antibody studies not high-yield). Risk factors: family history, increasing age, female. Confirm: ↑TSH, ↓free T4.

Start low, go slow. Tablets: 25, 50, 75, 88, 100, 112, 125, 137, 150, 175, 200, 300 mcg. Titration: check TSH every 4–8 weeks until euthyroid; TSH ≥4.0 → next dose up. Once stable: TSH only, annually and with major health changes.

Levothyroxine education ("a picky drug"): take with water on an empty stomach; interacts with other meds. Control affected by ≥10% weight change, taking with food/meds, missed or extra doses, antiepileptics and steroids, pregnancy (needs ↑ ~30%); biotin interferes with TSH measurement.

Hyperthyroidism: heat intolerance, warm moist skin, fine hand tremor, tachycardia/tachyarrhythmias, anxiety, irritability, ophthalmopathy (early or late in Graves). Refer all hyperthyroid patients; nonselective beta-blockers (propranolol) for symptoms while awaiting endocrinology.
USPSTF: identify adults with BMI >30. Measures: BMI and waist circumference (>40 in men, >35 in women).

Cotesting every 5 years (preferred); cytology every 3 years; or HPV every 5 years

blocks.text: Stop screening: total hysterectomy for benign reasons (no CIN2, CIN3, AIS or cancer history); age ≥65 with 3 negative Paps or 2 negative HPV tests in the last 10 years. Screen more often: HIV, immunocompromise, history of cervical cancer, in-utero DES exposure, prior abnormal cytology or positive HPV. Abnormal results rarely return to average-risk guidelines.

Pelvic exam tips: scant lubricant on the finger; press down while inserting; sweep to locate the cervix; introital tone guides speculum choice. Pap collection: sample the transformation zone and squamocolumnar junction; 360° clockwise rotation, never reverse direction; cervix brush 5 rotations; spatula 1 rotation; cytobrush 2–3 rotations (spatula followed by cytobrush, or broom alone).

rows: Reflex cytology; HPV 16/18 → colposcopy with biopsy

blocks.text: Inflammation with change in odor or discharge, itching and discomfort. Differential: BV, candidiasis, trichomoniasis, other STIs causing cervicitis. Self-diagnosis is often inaccurate.

rows: Multiple partners, no condoms, douching, HSV-2
Pregnancy, CHC, diabetes, weakened immunity, recent antibiotics
Multiple partners, no condoms, HIV, teens, older females
Metronidazole 500 mg BID ×7 days or gel daily ×5 days
Vaginal azole cream/ovule, or fluconazole 150 mg PO once

blocks.text: Recurrent candidiasis (e.g., 3 episodes in 4 months) → screen for immunocompromising conditions.
Perimenopause: transition to menopause; mean 4 years, median 7–10 years; can start in the mid-30s; low-estrogen states — hormone testing not useful.

rows: Irregular menses, "brain fog," sleep/mood changes, hot flashes and night sweats, osteoporosis risk, CV risk
Vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, urgency, frequency, recurrent UTIs

blocks.text: HRT is first-line: COC for perimenopausal patients wanting contraception; estrogen only after total hysterectomy; estrogen + progestin if uterus present; contraindications same as CHC. Nonhormonal (contraindications or preference): FDA-approved paroxetine (Brisdelle) 7.5 mg and fezolinetant 45 mg daily; off-label (NAMS-supported) citalopram, escitalopram, desvenlafaxine, venlafaxine, gabapentin. Lowest effective dose for the shortest time.

Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (vulvovaginal atrophy): low estrogen; pale, dry, smooth, shiny epithelium with loss of rugae; fragility/petechiae; dryness; abnormal discharge; pH >5. Management: moisturizers/lubricants; topical vaginal estrogen (cream, tablet, ring, capsule) preferred over systemic if only VVA; ospemifene (oral SERM; hot flashes common); vaginal DHEA (prasterone) daily.
Calcium ≥1,200 mg/day; vitamin D 800–1,000 IU/day (D3, cholecalciferol). Reduce smoking, alcohol, steroids; weight-bearing, balance and resistance exercise; fall prevention.

Risk factors: advanced age, prior fragility fracture, low body weight, parental hip fracture, RA, smoking, excess alcohol, early menopause, long-term glucocorticoids. FRAX = 10-year fracture probability. Screening: DEXA (gold standard) — all females ≥65; females and males of any age with risk factors.

Who gets drugs: osteopenia + ↑FRAX; osteopenia + fragility fracture; osteoporosis. First-line bisphosphonates: alendronate (Fosamax), risedronate (Actonel, Atelvia), ibandronate (Boniva), zoledronic acid (Reclast). Contraindications include bariatric surgery, hypocalcemia, Barrett esophagus. Alternatives: denosumab (Prolia) for intolerance/nonresponse — BMD drops rapidly when stopped, so another drug must start ASAP; raloxifene (SERM) for postmenopausal women who can't take the others. Duration: oral 5 years, IV 3 years. Follow-up DEXA individualized — when objectives are clear and results will change management (new risk factors/fracture, before stopping a bisphosphonate).
Resources: CDC Contraception app; ASCCP Management Guidelines app; STI Tx Guide; USPSTF app; Johns Hopkins Menopause Guide; FRAX; ACS breast cancer; NIH Breast Cancer Risk Assessment Tool.
Q1. Highest breast cancer risk: (1) 45-year-old, six pregnancies (2) 61-year-old nulliparous with dense breasts (3) 50-year-old with higher BMI (4) 32-year-old transgender female on HRT 2 years.

Q2. 28-year-old with worsening menstrual pain starting after a pregnancy 2 years ago: (1) normal after birth (2) an NSAID will eliminate it (3) suggests an underlying structural problem (4) lifestyle alone.
Q3. 23-year-old, overweight, irregular menses, hirsutism since puberty: (1) pelvic US required (2) fibroids (3) androgen tumor (4) PCOS criteria met.
Q4. Accurate contraception advice: (1) IUD can be used with a nulliparous cervix (2) COCs OK with prior DVT (3) LARC requires specialist insertion (4) no CHC while breastfeeding a 9-month-old.
Q5. 25-year-old with discharge and itching: (1) color/consistency determine cause (2) most likely candidiasis (3) STIs unlikely due to itching (4) more information needed.
Q6. Third candidiasis episode in 4 months: (1) douche (2) abstain 2 months (3) screen for immunocompromising conditions (4) remove Mirena.

Q7. Asian woman asks about osteoporosis risk: (1) sex and ethnicity lower risk (2) 3 glasses of wine/week increases risk (3) your spontaneous fracture puts you at higher risk (4) 120 lb is protective.
Q8. NOT a contraindication to alendronate: (1) bariatric surgery (2) hypocalcemia (3) postmenopausal (4) Barrett esophagus.

blocks.text: Covers prostate disorders (BPH, cancer, prostatitis), male sexual health, epididymitis, torsion, testicular cancer, varicocele, hydrocele, hernias, gynecomastia and Tanner stages.
Noncancerous prostate enlargement; 80% of men by age 80. Alpha receptors are abundant in the prostate, bladder base, prostate capsule and prostatic urethra.

LUTS: change in stream (force, caliber, splitting); hesitancy, postvoid dribbling; incontinence; frequency, urgency, nocturia; incomplete emptying, retention. Exam: firm, smooth, symmetrically enlarged prostate; elevated PSA. Hematuria is not a typical BPH finding. Untreated complication: recurrent UTIs (and retention).

rows: ↓bladder outlet obstruction; caution orthostatic hypotension; selective alpha blockers were originally BP drugs
Shrink the prostate; 6–12 months for full benefit; get baseline PSA first
Relaxes bladder outlet and prostate smooth muscle
No renal/hepatic precautions; sulfa allergy precaution

blocks.text: Most common cancer in men; lifetime risk 16%; risk of dying 2.9%. Risk factors: older age; Black men; family history (first-degree relative, diagnosed <65); BRCA1/BRCA2. Men with risk factors benefit most from screening.

Screening principles: risk-based assessment at 40; PSA at 50–55, every 1–2 years; shared decision-making; only with ≥10 years' life expectancy; usually stop at 70–75; DRE no longer recommended for screening; screening is for asymptomatic patients.

rows: Ejaculation (within 24 h), DRE (clinically insignificant), cycling, prostate infection, prostate massage

blocks.text: Assessment: most are asymptomatic at diagnosis; may have new ED or obstructive symptoms. PSA sensitivity 21%, specificity 91%; PSA >4 is suspicious; a PSA value doesn't rule cancer in or out. DRE asymmetry, induration or nodularity is suspicious even with a normal PSA. A rising PSA on finasteride is suspicious (5-ARIs should lower it).

Acute bacterial prostatitis: usually ascending infection (urethritis, cystitis, epididymitis). Gram-negatives (E. coli, Proteus); STIs (C. trachomatis, Ureaplasma, T. vaginalis). History: acute pain in perineum, lower abdomen, testicles or penile tip; pain with ejaculation and/or defecation; frequency, urgency, dysuria, nocturia; fever, chills, malaise, myalgias. Exam: enlarged, firm or boggy, exquisitely tender prostate — avoid vigorous massage; check CVA tenderness. UA/culture: hematuria, cloudy, pyuria/bacteriuria, leukocytosis; STI tests if at risk; PSA elevated.

Management: antibiotics 2–6 weeks (empiric pending C&S). No STI risk: ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin or TMP-SMX. STI risk: ceftriaxone 1 g + 2 weeks of doxycycline. Symptoms improve in 2–6 days; negative UA at 7 days predicts cure if the full course is completed. Defer PSA screening 1 month after treatment.

Chronic bacterial prostatitis: often untreated/undertreated acute prostatitis; subtle, variable pain, frequency, urgency; exam usually normal; empiric antibiotics 4–6 weeks; urine culture; possibly NSAIDs or alpha blocker. Low threshold for urology referral.

Diminished libido (often with sexual/voiding disorders); ejaculatory disorders (premature, delayed, retrograde, anorgasmia); erectile dysfunction (acquiring/sustaining, rigidity, duration). Get a good sexual history.

rows: Medications, microvascular disease, neurologic disorders, OSA, CKD, drug use, smoking, hypo/hyperthyroidism, prostate cancer
Depression, stress, relationship issues. Nocturnal erections present → consider psychogenic

blocks.text: Medical evaluation: H&P (95% sensitive, 50% specific); nocturnal penile tumescence testing; duplex Doppler; CBC, TSH, PSA, hormone levels.

PDE-5 inhibitors (ED and LUTS): sildenafil (Viagra); avanafil (Stendra) — fastest acting; tadalafil (Cialis) — longest acting, also for BPH; vardenafil (Levitra, Staxyn). Caution in CVD. Contraindicated with nitrates (e.g., isosorbide).

rows: Fatigue, hair loss, ↓lean muscle, obesity, gynecomastia

blocks.text: Testosterone therapy improves sexual function and libido, muscle mass, mood, anemia, insulin sensitivity, bone density.

Low T (<300 ng/dL) algorithm: clinical suspicion → total T at 8–10 a.m. → normal = eugonadal. Low → repeat total T + LH + FSH → low T with normal LH/FSH = secondary hypogonadism → refer to endocrinology; low T with elevated LH/FSH = primary hypogonadism → consider testosterone.

rows: Epididymal tenderness; if STI, positive culture or urethritis

blocks.text: Epididymitis: noninfectious causes most common — urine reflux into ejaculatory ducts/vas, prolonged sitting, congenital defect. Infectious is rare unless STI (75% C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae; chlamydia most common). Gradual scrotal pain, dysuria; epididymis very tender, enlarged, indurated; urethral discharge with gonorrhea; positive Prehn sign. Diagnostics: UA + culture (normal if noninfectious; pyuria = infectious); NAAT; ultrasound if no improvement or uncertain. Management: noninfectious — rest, fluids, scrotal support, ice, NSAIDs/analgesics. Infectious — gonorrhea: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM; chlamydia: doxycycline 100 mg BID ×10 days. Improvement within 3 days; resolution in 2–4 weeks.
Testicular torsion: twisting of testis and spermatic cord → ischemia if not corrected.

sections.title: Testicular cancer and other scrotal concerns

blocks.text: Testicular cancer: males 15–35; history of cryptorchidism (even after orchiopexy; either testis, greater risk in the undescended one). Encourage self-exam. Diagnose with scrotal ultrasound; refer to urology; discuss sperm cryopreservation.

Varicocele: swollen veins, "bag of worms"; painful or asymptomatic; can lower sperm count/quality. Hydrocele: fluid around the testicle; common in infants and resolves; in adults benign or pathologic; transilluminates.

Inguinal hernias: most common hernia type; more common in males; ⅔ right-sided. Groin lump that disappears supine. Clinical diagnosis; ultrasound if unclear. Athletes with an inguinal hernia → refer to a general surgeon.

Gynecomastia: benign glandular proliferation of the male breast; asymptomatic or tender. Differential: pseudogynecomastia (obesity, no well-defined rubbery mass); breast cancer (unilateral, nontender, hard, immobile, off-center from the nipple).

Tanner stages (male) are shown pictorially: stage 1 prepubertal; stage 2 testicular enlargement, sparse hair at penile base; stage 3 penis lengthens, darker curlier hair; stage 4 penis widens, abundant coarse hair; stage 5 adult size and distribution. Small penis (<4 cm), small testes and scant hair in a late adolescent → refer for delayed puberty.
Q1. NOT common in BPH: (1) nocturia (2) postvoid dribbling (3) hematuria (4) weak stream.
Q2. Complication of untreated BPH: (1) prostate cancer (2) rhabdomyolysis (3) varicocele (4) recurrent UTIs.
Q3. True for new BPH: (1) BPH drugs block alpha receptors in the prostate (2) alpha antagonists rarely used (3) baseline PSA not needed before 5-ARI (4) alpha blocker + 5-ARI contraindicated.
Q4. 70-year-old with LUTS — least likely cause: (1) prostate cancer (2) prostatitis (3) UTI (4) BPH.

Q5. Does NOT warrant urology referral: (1) 48-year-old with DRE nodules/induration, PSA 3.5 (2) 55-year-old on finasteride, PSA 2.8 → 3.3 (3) 45-year-old with ED, PSA 4.4 (4) 60-year-old with acute prostatitis, PSA 6.0.
Q6. 45-year-old with fever, dysuria, bilateral pelvic pain, pain with BMs: (1) uncomplicated UTI (2) nephrolithiasis (3) pyelonephritis (4) acute bacterial prostatitis.
Q7. NOT an ED risk factor: (1) CVD (2) neurologic issues (3) history of gonorrhea (4) antidepressants.
Q8. Absolute contraindication to a PDE-5 inhibitor: (1) losartan (2) isosorbide (3) tamsulosin (4) dapagliflozin.
Q9. 36-year-old bus driver, testicular pain and swelling after a 12-hour shift, gradually worse: (1) acute prostatitis (2) prostate cancer (3) chronic prostatitis (4) epididymitis.

Q10. 19-year-old kneed in groin 3 h ago; severe pain, N/V; right testicle tender, hard, swollen; negative cremasteric reflex: (1) assess for hernia (2) calculate TWIST and refer to ED (3) UA and culture (4) KUB.
Q11. NOT associated with testicular cancer: (1) unilateral swelling (2) painless firm nodule (3) cryptorchidism (4) hernia repair.
Q12. 44-year-old with mild left groin discomfort exercising; lump disappears supine: (1) ventral (2) umbilical (3) inguinal (4) incarcerated hernia.
Q13. 20-year-old athlete with inguinal hernia: (1) restrict all activity (2) refer to general surgeon (3) truss (4) defer surgery unless entrapped.
Q14. Late adolescent with groin itching; penis <4 cm, small testes, scant pubic hair: (1) follow up in 1 year (2) hygiene (3) refer for delayed puberty (4) ask about sexual activity.

blocks.text: Three orthopedic principles

items: If the pain is orthopedic, it should be reproducible. Pain that isn't reproducible points to an extrinsic cause.
Joints are made to move. Rest, but keep joints moving.
When in doubt, send it out: refer to a specialist or order more imaging.

rows: Degenerative: worn cartilage, bone spurs, bony remodeling
Autoimmune: thickened synovial membrane, bone loss, worn cartilage
Any joint; may be unilateral or bilateral (knees, hips, spine, hands)
Limited ROM, tenderness, crepitus, possible effusion
Ulnar deviation, boutonnière and swan-neck deformities

blocks.text: Tip: Bouchard nodes are BELOW Heberden nodes; Heberden nodes sit HIGHER (DIP). RA and OA both affect the hands, so know the differences.
Diagnosing OA is clinical: pain in one or a few joints, age ≥45, and morning stiffness ≤60 min. A radiograph supports the diagnosis if it shows joint-space narrowing and/or osteophytes.

Treating OA: nonpharmacologic measures come first. These include patient education, aerobic and strengthening exercise, weight loss if appropriate, and heat, cold, ultrasound or acupuncture, which help some patients.
OA pharmacologic management, ONLY as needed
NSAID cautions include heart failure, CVD, GI bleed and renal impairment.
RA workup

items: Rheumatoid factor (RF)
Anti-CCP antibodies against citrullinated peptides/proteins. These have higher specificity than RF and similar sensitivity.
Acute-phase reactants: ESR, CRP
ANA: a negative result may exclude SLE
CBC, LFTs, BUN, Cr, uric acid, UA

blocks.text: RA: 2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria. Diagnosis needs ≥6/10 points.
Fibromyalgia is a noninflammatory condition with soft-tissue tenderness, typically between ages 20 and 55. It is not a diagnosis of exclusion, though differentials must be excluded.
Assessment

items: Widespread Pain Index (WPI): 19 painful body regions, 1 point per region, maximum 19.
Symptom Severity (SS) scale: maximum 12. Each item is scored 0 (no problem), 1 (mild), 2 (moderate) or 3 (severe):
Degree of fatigue
Waking unrefreshed
Cognitive symptoms ("fibro fog")
Somatic symptoms (abdominal cramping, IBS symptoms, headache, depression, etc.)

blocks.text: Diagnosis, ACR 2016 criteria. All three must be met:

items: (WPI ≥7 and SS ≥5) OR (WPI 4–6 and SS ≥9)
AND symptoms present for >3 months
AND differentials excluded

blocks.text: Initial management: patient education, sleep hygiene, and treating comorbid mood and sleep disorders. Exercise should include aerobic conditioning, stretching and strengthening. Medications for pain include amitriptyline, duloxetine and pregabalin, among others.
Key anatomy:

items: Joints: acromioclavicular (AC), glenohumeral, sternoclavicular
Rotator cuff, "SITS": supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis
Subacromial bursa: lies between the acromion and the humeral head

blocks.text: Assessment of shoulder pain (algorithm)

items: Is the pain reproducible?
No. Consider an extrinsic cause: cholecystitis, MI, radiculopathy, zoster.
Yes, with acute trauma. Get imaging ± referral. Differentials include AC joint separation and clavicle fracture.
Yes, no trauma. Is there weakness or impaired ROM?
Yes: glenohumeral cause, such as rotator cuff tendinopathy or adhesive capsulitis.
No: extra-glenohumeral cause, such as biceps tendinopathy or AC joint OA.

blocks.text: Tip: Take a thorough history, develop your differentials, then make the diagnosis.
Shoulder-specific tests

items: Rotator cuff tendinopathy: drop arm test, Jobe (empty can) test
Shoulder impingement: Neer test, Hawkins–Kennedy test

rows: Pain with impingement: at 90° mild, at 60–70° moderate, at 45° severe
Examiner raises the arm overhead while pressing down to prevent a shrug
Straight arm, 90° abduction, 30° forward flexion, internal rotation; adduction against resistance
Patient lowers the arm from full abduction
Can't lower the arm smoothly. A sudden drop with pain means a full-thickness tear.
Weakness on external rotation against resistance

blocks.text: Example: a painter whose lateral deltoid hurts when raising the arm overhead after 6 weeks of work, with a positive empty can test, likely has supraspinatus tendinitis (rotator cuff tendinopathy).

This is inflammation of the extensor tendons of the posterior forearm where they attach to the lateral epicondyle. It comes from repetitive motion of the forearm extensors; a carpenter with elbow and proximal forearm pain, worse with movement and no trauma, is the classic case.
Management: rest but keep the joint moving, ice, NSAIDs, counterforce bracing, steroid injections and physical therapy.
The scaphoid stabilizes the midcarpal joint and gets its blood supply from the radial artery. It is the most commonly injured wrist bone, usually from a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH).
Signs of fracture are deep, dull wrist pain that is worse with gripping or squeezing, and anatomic snuffbox tenderness. Scaphoid fractures carry a high risk of avascular necrosis.

rows: PA, lateral, oblique and scaphoid-view radiographs. If negative, get MRI or CT. If MRI isn't available, repeat radiographs in 7–14 days.
Suspected fracture not confirmed on radiograph. Confirmed fracture on radiograph or MRI: immobilization up to 5 months.
Any confirmed fracture (displaced or not), delayed presentation (>3 weeks), carpal instability

blocks.text: Tip: Initial imaging can be falsely negative. When you're suspicious, immobilize, repeat the imaging and refer. A missed scaphoid fracture can lead to avascular necrosis, with chronic pain, deformity and disability.
Differential diagnosis
Physical exam

items: Inspect, palpate and percuss the spine.
Check gait, including heel-to-toe walking.
Do a neurologic exam: motor, sensory, reflexes.

Assess for radiculopathy with a straight leg raise (SLR). Raise the patient's extended leg with the ankle dorsiflexed. The test is positive if sciatica is reproduced between 10° and 60° on the affected side.

blocks.text: Imaging

headers: Pain lasting >4 weeks, or no response to conservative treatment
rows: For most conditions; a radiograph may be needed first
Neurologic deficits (extremity weakness, loss of DTRs, sensory deficit, bowel/bladder incontinence); suspected neoplasm (e.g., metastasis); infection (fever, IV drug use, immunocompromise)

blocks.text: Management

items: Nonpharmacologic: heat, physical therapy, massage
Pharmacologic: systemic NSAIDs ± muscle relaxants
Not indicated: opioids, antidepressants, steroids, antiepileptics
Expected course: 90% of LBP resolves within 4–6 weeks.

blocks.text: Cauda equina syndrome is an emergency.

items: Marked neurologic disability with saddle anesthesia: numbness between the legs and around the anus and genitals, and inability to feel toilet paper.
Bladder: urinary retention or incontinence, difficulty starting urination, loss of sensation when passing urine.
Bowel: incontinence, constipation, loss of sensation during a bowel movement.
Sexual: erectile or ejaculatory dysfunction, loss of sensation during intercourse.
Etiology: neural tube defects, infection, inflammation, mass, lumbar spinal stenosis, injury, herniated disc.

blocks.text: The character, location and pattern of the pain point to the diagnosis.

rows: Worse with use, better with rest

blocks.text: A 30-year-old patient presents with knee pain after a fall 24 hours ago. There is diffuse tenderness and mild swelling of the knee. The patient is able to ambulate in the office with minimal difficulty. How should this patient be 1. Orthopedic referral 2. Radiograph of the knee 3. Supportive treatment 4. MRI of the knee TIP: Not every patient needs imaging! Follow the rules.
Key anatomy: ACL, PCL, MCL, LCL, medial and lateral menisci, fibular head.
Tip: Not every patient needs imaging. Follow the rules.
Ottawa Knee Rules. Get a knee radiograph if any one of these is present:

items: Age >55
Unable to bear weight immediately after the injury and for 4 steps in the office
Isolated patellar tenderness
Fibular head tenderness
Unable to flex the knee to 90°

blocks.text: Example: a 30-year-old with diffuse tenderness and mild swelling 24 hours after a fall, who can walk in the office, meets none of the rules. Treat with supportive care.
Knee tests

rows: Flex the knee 20–30°; translate the tibia anteriorly
Flex the knee to 90°; translate the tibia anteriorly
No end feel, or more anterior translation than the other side
Flex the knee to 90°; push the tibia posteriorly
No end feel, or excessive posterior translation
Passively flex and extend the knee; repeat with the tibia internally, then externally, rotated
Popping, joint-line pain, or limited ROM
Prone, knee at 90°; stabilize the thigh, press the heel down while rotating the foot internally and externally
Slight hip flexion and abduction, knee flexed; apply gentle inward stress with hands over the lateral knee and proximal tibia
Same position; apply gentle outward stress

blocks.text: Memory aid: Valgus means an inward force that stresses the MCL: knees "grow" together (knock-kneed). Varus means an outward force that stresses the LCL: knees go "round" outward (bow-legged).

Popliteal (Baker) cyst is a fluid-filled sac that swells the popliteal fossa. Synovial fluid flows from the knee joint into the gastrocnemio-semimembranosus bursa. Most are asymptomatic and found incidentally on ultrasound or MRI. They are associated with OA, inflammatory joint disease and injury.
Ottawa Ankle Rules

rows: Unable to bear weight immediately after the injury or for 4 steps in the office
Bony tenderness in the malleolar zone: the posterior edge or tip of the lateral or medial malleolus (distal 6 cm)
Bony tenderness in the midfoot: navicular or base of the 5th metatarsal

blocks.text: Ankle sprain is stretching or partial tearing of the lateral or deltoid ligaments.

items: Lateral sprain is most common. It is an inversion injury of the plantarflexed foot (anterior talofibular and calcaneofibular ligaments).
Medial sprain is rare. It is an eversion injury of the deltoid ligament, the strongest ankle ligament.

rows: Larger but incomplete tear. Most common sprain in primary care. Some joint instability, restricted ROM, painful walking.

blocks.text: Management: PRICE plus early mobility

items: Protection: elastic bandage, splint, walking boot, air cast
Rest: limit weight bearing until gait is normal
Ice: ice or cold water for 15–20 min every 2–3 h for 48 h
Compression: elastic bandage for support, applied early to minimize swelling
Elevation: to reduce swelling
Analgesics: acetaminophen and NSAIDs

blocks.text: The chapter outline also lists plantar fasciitis and Morton neuroma under ankle/foot.

items: Symptoms: severe pain, redness, warmth and swelling, with onset more often at night.
Presentation and risk factors, "Ma'am":
Monoarticular: the first MTP is most common, then the knee
Atraumatic
Alcohol
Meats and meds: thiazide and loop diuretics, recently started urate-lowering therapy, seafood, liver, red meat
Confirmatory test: synovial fluid analysis, which shows negatively birefringent, needle-shaped urate crystals.

blocks.text: Acute flare treatment, chosen by patient characteristics:

items: Colchicine: avoid with renal or hepatic impairment
NSAIDs: avoid with CVD, GI bleed or renal impairment
Glucocorticoids: intra-articular, intramuscular or oral

blocks.text: Start urate-lowering therapy (ULT) if any of these apply:

items: ≥2 flares a year
Intolerance of acute medications
Tophi, or damage on radiograph

blocks.text: Allopurinol is first-line ULT. Give anti-inflammatory prophylaxis for 3–6 months after starting ULT. For a third flare within 12 months, the plan is allopurinol plus an anti-inflammatory.

rows: Pain at the base of the thumb with ulnar deviation of the wrist
De Quervain tenosynovitis. Finkelstein test: tuck the thumb inside the palm, make a fist, then deviate the wrist down (ulnar). Pain means a positive test.
Both wrists held in forced flexion for 30–60 s
Phalen test, for carpal tunnel syndrome
Tinel sign, for carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve compression)
Fluid-filled sac swelling the popliteal fossa

items: Arthritis: OA, RA, gout
Lower extremity: foot, ankle, knee, hip
Upper extremity: shoulder, elbow, wrist, hand
Sprain, strain, tendinitis, bursitis
Causes of low back pain
For each condition, know the predisposing factors, presenting signs and symptoms, red flags, how to diagnose (radiograph, clinical exam) and how to treat.

blocks.text: Q13.1 What is the first-line pharmacologic management of osteoarthritis?

items: Acetaminophen 2. NSAIDs 3. Opioids 4. Duloxetine

blocks.text: Q13.2 A patient with osteoarthritis asks if it is safe to take meloxicam daily for pain. This medication may be unsafe if the patient has which of the following conditions?

items: Heart failure 2. Depression 3. Hypothyroidism 4. COPD

blocks.text: Q13.3 Which of the following is a FALSE statement about fibromyalgia?

items: It is an inflammatory condition. 2. It causes tenderness to soft tissues. 3. It typically occurs between the ages of 20 and 55 years. 4. It is a diagnosis of exclusion.

blocks.text: Q13.4 A patient started a new job as a painter. After 6 weeks of work, they report pain in the lateral deltoid when raising the arm overhead. The NP elicits a positive empty can test. Which of the following is suspected?

blocks.text: The skin has three layers:

items: Epidermis: the barrier
Dermis: handles tensile load and contains nerves
Hypodermis: insulation, energy and fluid storage

rows: Deep infection; a localized collection of pus
Deep infection of a hair follicle
Flat change in skin color (brown, blue, red or hypopigmented)
Solid lesion >0.5–2.0 cm; over 2.0 cm it is a tumor
Raised, solid lesion ≤0.5 cm; color varies

blocks.text: Approach to dermatology

items: Know the anatomy: which layer is affected? Take an OLD CARTS history.
Use pattern recognition on exam: texture, plane, depth, color, borders, shape, blanching and distribution.
Ask whether this is a skin problem or a systemic problem.

blocks.text: Tip: Document a detailed description so other clinicians can "see" the lesion from your notes.
Pharmacology and skin

items: Choose the route: topical, or systemic (oral or IV).
Supportive care is enough for some conditions; not every condition needs medication.
When unsure: "If it's wet, make it dry. If it's dry, make it wet."
Bacteria: gram-positive organisms, usually Staph or Strep
Fungi, two main types: dermatophytes (tinea) and Candida. Tinea versicolor is caused by a yeast.
Viruses: herpes, HPV, molluscum contagiosum, HIV, plantar warts, varicella, viral exanthems
Infestations (parasites)

blocks.text: Single lesion, definitive diagnosis requires Not experienced by multiple members of Bites inject toxins that cause swelling and inflammation; some spider bites cause tissue necrosis or systemic neurologic symptoms. visualization of the spider. brown recluse bite image TIP: Spider bites often mistaken for MRSA abscesses, herpes zoster, Lyme disease
Impetigo is a superficial infection caused by Streptococcus, Staphylococcus or both. The classic description is "honey-colored crusts", often around the mouth. Treat topically.
Ecthyma is the deep, ulcerative form of impetigo and needs oral antibiotics.
Cellulitis is a bacterial infection of the dermis and hypodermis, caused by group A Streptococcus and Staph aureus.

items: Signs: erythema with poorly circumscribed margins, edema, tenderness, warmth; possibly fever and elevated WBC.
Nonpurulent cellulitis: oral dicloxacillin, cephalexin, amoxicillin/clavulanate or clindamycin.

blocks.text: Tip: Deep, nonpurulent infection plus systemic symptoms means systemic antibiotics.
Abscess. In a student athlete with a 2-cm abscess, think MRSA. The treatment is incision and drainage.
Tip: "When there's pus about, let it out!"

Folliculitis is inflammation of hair follicles, superficial or deep. It presents as pustules and/or papules at the follicles. It is usually Staph (sometimes Strep pyogenes). Recent hot tub use: think Pseudomonas.
Bacterial skin infections: treatment per IDSA

rows: I&D first-line; TMP-SMX, clindamycin, tetracycline, linezolid (5–10 days)
I&D first-line. Antibiotics if fever, cellulitis >2.5 cm, systemic symptoms or failed initial treatment
MSSA: dicloxacillin, cephalexin. MRSA: doxycycline, clindamycin or TMP-SMX
Topical: mupirocin or clindamycin gel. Oral: cephalexin, dicloxacillin QID. MRSA: doxycycline or TMP-SMX. Pseudomonas: ciprofloxacin

blocks.text: Bites can lead to bacterial infection from two sources:

items: The biter's oral flora. Dog or cat: Pasteurella. Human: Staph, Strep, anaerobes.
The patient's skin flora: Staph and Strep are most common.

blocks.text: The antibiotic of choice is amoxicillin/clavulanate (Augmentin).
Management

items: Clean and copiously irrigate.
Antibiotic prophylaxis with amoxicillin/clavulanate for 3–5 days if any of these apply:
Immunocompromised
Suture closure
Involvement of bones, joints, hands, face or genitals
Deep puncture wounds
Human bites
Tetanus prophylaxis if the last dose was more than 5 years ago.

blocks.text: Rabies prophylaxis indications

items: High-risk animals: skunks, raccoons, foxes, bats
Atypically aggressive behavior (e.g., squirrels, beavers)
The animal can't be obtained for testing
Vaccination status unknown

blocks.text: Refer emergently for rabies immune globulin (HRIG) and the multidose rabies vaccine series. Rabies is a reportable condition.

rows: Pruritic, scaling border, spreads centrifugally, central clearing
Pruritic, erythematous base, white patches, burning, satellite lesions

items: Tinea unguium (onychomycosis) needs oral therapy, not a topical antifungal.
Differential for a scaly, circumscribed, erythematous truncal lesion with central clearing: tinea corporis, eczema, the herald patch of pityriasis rosea. Cellulitis does not fit.

items: Viral exanthems are characteristic skin lesions of viral illness (measles, rubella, varicella).
Viral enanthems are oral eruptions before, with or after an exanthem, such as Koplik spots in measles.
Common viruses with skin findings:
HPV: common and plantar warts
Molluscum contagiosum: 2–5 mm umbilicated papules
HSV-1 and HSV-2
Herpes zoster (shingles)
Sexually transmitted: HPV (genital warts), genital HSV, HIV (acute exanthem and infectious or neoplastic conditions).

Zoster presents as painful, clustered vesicles in a dermatomal distribution (e.g., T4 across the chest) that do not cross the midline. It is very painful and has a prodrome.
Pain: NSAIDs for mild to moderate pain, opioids for severe pain.
Antiviral therapy

items: <72 hours from onset: oral acyclovir, famciclovir, valacyclovir (or brivudine) for 7 days.
>72 hours: treat only if new lesions are still appearing or the patient is immunocompromised.

blocks.text: Tip: If the patient is immunocompromised, ALWAYS prescribe antivirals, regardless of time since onset.

rows: Ear pain, vesicles in the ear, ipsilateral facial paralysis. Refer to ENT.
Pain lasting more than 4 months in the same dermatome

blocks.text: Shingrix (recombinant zoster vaccine, RZV), per CDC:

items: Immunocompetent adults ≥50; immunocompromised adults ≥19.
2 IM doses, 2–6 months apart. Immunocompromised patients may get them 1–2 months apart.
It is a recombinant (not live) vaccine, safer and more effective than Zostavax (live). Give it regardless of Zostavax history.
Give it after the acute episode resolves.

blocks.text: Spiders. Bites inject toxins that cause swelling and inflammation. Some (e.g., brown recluse) cause tissue necrosis or systemic neurologic symptoms. Typically there is a single lesion, and it doesn't affect several household members. A definitive diagnosis requires seeing the spider.
Tip: Spider bites are often mistaken for MRSA abscesses, herpes zoster or Lyme disease.
Ticks

items: Symptoms appear 2–14 days after exposure. Transmission requires about 36 hours of attachment.
Lyme disease is transmitted most often. It causes erythema migrans ("bull's-eye" rash).
Other tick-borne diseases: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF), with a diffuse rash that includes the palms and soles; babesiosis; ehrlichiosis.

rows: Doxycycline 100 mg BID × 10 days, OR amoxicillin, OR cefuroxime
Doxycycline is the only recommended treatment for RMSF.
PEP is not recommended for RMSF.

blocks.text: PEP checklist. All must apply:

items: Endemic area
Tick removed within 72 hours
Engorged tick
Ixodes (deer) tick
Doxycycline is safe for the patient

blocks.text: Bed bugs. Pruritic erythematous papules 2–5 mm. The reaction varies from immediate to 10 days later. Untreated, they resolve in about 1 week. Diagnosis requires finding the bed bugs.
Scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei mite)

items: Symptoms appear 3–6 weeks after exposure. Spread is skin to skin, not animal to human.
Intensely pruritic small erythematous papules with burrows.
Distribution: sides and webs of the fingers, wrists, axillae, areolae, genitalia, waist.
Treatment: topical permethrin cream. Safe for age >2 months and in pregnancy and lactation. Apply to the entire body (except the head) once; may repeat in 2 weeks.

blocks.text: Pediculosis (lice)

items: Distribution: head (capitis, most common), body (corporis), pubic hair (pubis, sexually transmitted).
Treatment: topical permethrin or malathion. Wet combing with proper technique every 3–4 days for at least 3 weeks is a reasonable alternative.

blocks.text: The manual shows images of four dermatitis types. The descriptions below come from standard references:

items: Eczema (atopic dermatitis): pruritic, dry, erythematous patches, often flexural in older children and adults.
Psoriasis: well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees).
Seborrheic dermatitis: greasy, yellowish scale on the scalp (dandruff), eyebrows and nasolabial folds.
Contact dermatitis: erythema, often vesicular, sharply limited to the area of contact.

blocks.text: How topical steroids work

items: They work by causing vasoconstriction.
Potency is the amount of drug needed for an effect. It depends on the vasoconstriction produced, the immunosuppressive effects and the vehicle.
The vehicle is the medium that carries the drug.

rows: Thick or hyperkeratotic lesions; avoid in hairy areas
Less residue, dries quickly; skin folds and acute inflammation
Hairy areas; less occlusive, dries quickly
Ideal for the scalp, but expensive

items: Benign: seborrheic keratosis, skin tags, polyps, cysts, lipoma, many others
Premalignant: actinic keratosis
Malignant: basal cell carcinoma (BCC), squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), melanoma

blocks.text: Lesion evaluation: ABCDE

items: Asymmetry: one half doesn't match the other
Border: irregular, not smooth
Color: more than one color in the lesion
Diameter: >6 mm (pencil eraser)
Evolving: the mole is changing

blocks.text: Refer lesions highly suspicious for malignancy. Do a punch or shave biopsy for lesions of uncertain cause with low suspicion of malignancy.

Seborrheic keratosis is a benign, brown, warty lesion with a "stuck-on" look, usually on the chest, back or scalp. It may get irritated and bleed. There may be one or many, often a cosmetic concern. Treat symptomatic lesions with cryotherapy, curettage/shave excision or electrodesiccation, and biopsy suspicious ones.
Actinic (solar) keratosis is a precancerous scaling macule, papule or plaque in sun-exposed areas. It may progress to SCC, and there's no way to predict which will.

items: Treatment: destructive therapy (liquid nitrogen cryosurgery, shave excision) or topicals (5-fluorouracil, imiquimod).
Refer for biopsy if indurated; painful, ulcerated or bleeding; or hyperkeratotic/hypertrophic and not resolving or recurring after standard therapy.

rows: Pearly pink-red or flesh-colored nodule with telangiectasia; may be scaly. Painless. Shoulders, chest, face, back. Light skin, sun exposure, tanning beds, genetics.
Variable: plaque, crusting, ulceration, bleeding; flesh-toned to erythematous. Face, neck, scalp, extremities. Risks: sun exposure, actinic keratosis.

The "ugly duckling" lesion that differs from the patient's other nevi. Violates ABCDE, especially if changing or >6 mm. Sensory change, itch or inflammation. Legs, upper back, sun-exposed areas. Brown/black longitudinal streak in a nail (great toe, thumb). Risks: family history, tanning beds, sun.

blocks.text: A suspicious pigmented lesion is referred for excisional biopsy first. Don't punch-biopsy it or freeze it in the office.
SLE is a multisystem autoimmune disease, more common in Black, Asian and Hispanic women of childbearing age.

items: Manifestations: joint and muscle pain, fatigue, hair loss, thrombocytopenia, mouth sores, nervous system problems, lung or heart inflammation, abdominal pain, kidney involvement, skin rash, retinal problems, fever.
Malar ("butterfly") rash: an erythematous, maculopapular rash across the cheeks and nasal bridge, often brought on by sun exposure.
A positive ANA is the required entry criterion for the diagnostic criteria.

blocks.text: Erysipelas: well-demarcated bright red rash with raised edges in a toxic-looking patient; caused Necrotizing fasciitis: rare, rapidly progressing skin infection; red/purple skin, severe pain and Multisystem autoimmune disease (More common in Black, Asian, Hispanic females of childbearing age) Which of the following is a required component of the diagnostic criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus? 1. Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 2. Positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) test 3. Presence of malar rash 4. Positive of antiphospholipid antibodies test Dermatologic Emergencies NOTES If you see these, refer ASAP! by Streptococcus pyogenes fever, necrosis of affected area

items: Erysipelas: a well-demarcated, bright red rash with raised edges in a toxic-looking patient, caused by Streptococcus pyogenes.
Necrotizing fasciitis: a rare, rapidly progressing infection with red or purple skin, pain out of proportion, fever and necrosis.
Stevens–Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN):
A severe mucocutaneous reaction with extensive necrosis and detachment of the epidermis, caused by a medication or infection.
Prodrome: fever >102°F (38.9°C) and flu-like symptoms for 1–3 days.
Lesions: target lesions with central dusky purpura, possibly bullae and blisters. They spread from the face downward and involve the mucous membranes.
A positive Nikolsky sign (skin exfoliates with rubbing) may be present.
Antibiotics for skin infections
Diseases that present with vesicles/bullae, papules/macules, pustules/purulence, nodules and plaques
Dermatologic emergencies; systemic conditions with skin signs
For each, know the presentation, diagnosis, differential, drug and non-drug management, follow-up, normal course and when to refer.
