blocks.text: ARS is symptomatic inflammation of the paranasal sinuses (frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, maxillary).
Causes: viruses (most common); bacteria (<2% of cases); fungi (rare); allergies; irritants; dry air; GERD.

rows: Facial pain or pressure, worse bending forward
Purulent posterior pharyngeal or nasal secretions

blocks.text: Acute viral rhinosinusitis

items: Causes: rhinovirus, parainfluenza, RSV, etc.
Course: symptoms peak on days 3–6 and resolve in 10–14 days.
Definitions: acute <4 weeks; chronic >12 weeks.

rows: Not recommended: may overdry the mucosa. Consider if allergic rhinitis is present.

blocks.text: Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS) is a secondary bacterial infection. Suspect it with any of these patterns:

items: Persistent: ≥10 days without improvement
Severe: at onset and lasting at least 3 days (fever, purulent discharge, ill appearance)
Worsening, "double-sickening": symptoms improve, then worsen again

blocks.text: Pathogens: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis. Complications include orbital cellulitis and meningitis.
Treatment

items: Amoxicillin or amoxicillin/clavulanate × 5–7 days.
Recent antibiotic exposure: high-dose amoxicillin/clavulanate ER (2000/125 mg BID).
Penicillin allergy: doxycycline or a third-generation cephalosporin.

blocks.text: Allergic rhinitis is inflammation of the nasal mucous membranes.

items: Symptoms: sneezing, rhinorrhea, postnasal drip, congestion, nasal and mucosal itching, infraorbital edema (allergic shiners), allergic conjunctivitis.
Exam: pale, boggy, bluish-gray turbinates.

blocks.text: Management

items: Intranasal glucocorticoids (fluticasone, mometasone, beclomethasone): preferred monotherapy for persistent nasal and conjunctival symptoms.
Intranasal antihistamines (azelastine, olopatadine): better than oral antihistamines.
Second-generation oral antihistamines (fexofenadine, loratadine, cetirizine): less sedating than first-generation.
Intranasal decongestant (oxymetazoline): helps with severe congestion when given before the intranasal steroid or antihistamine.
Systemic corticosteroids: only for very severe or intractable symptoms.
Oral decongestants and leukotriene receptor antagonists: risks may outweigh benefits. Montelukast carries a boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events, including suicidal thoughts.

blocks.text: Decongestant adverse effects

items: Pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine (systemic)
Contraindicated: uncontrolled hypertension; MAOI therapy within 14 days.
Use caution with: closed-angle glaucoma, CAD, hyperthyroidism, urinary retention.
Misuse potential: stimulant use by athletes; illegal methamphetamine production.
Oxymetazoline (local): overuse causes rhinitis medicamentosa (rebound congestion).
Anterior (90%): from Kiesselbach plexus, an anastomosis of five major arteries.
Posterior (5–10%): in older patients, hard to control. Refer to the ER.
Bimodal: children and older adults.
Causes:
Idiopathic (most common)
Nose picking (epistaxis digitorum) or trauma
Foreign body (children, dementia)
Alcohol, cocaine
Infection, allergies
Bleeding disorder, anticoagulation and hypertension, which raise the risk of a posterior or severe bleed

blocks.text: Management

items: Refer if the patient is hemodynamically unstable or the bleed is severe (>30 min, or recurrent over 24 h).
Nasal compression: pinch the nose tightly for ≥5 minutes.
Topical decongestant: oxymetazoline.
Cautery: with the bleed visualized, using a silver nitrate stick.
Nasal packing.
Viral: 50–80% of cases, usually common-cold viruses. Less often HIV, CMV, EBV.
Bacterial (less common): group A Streptococcus (GAS) and other respiratory bacteria.
Noninfectious: GERD, dry air, smoke.

blocks.text: Strep pharyngitis accounts for 5–15% of adult cases. The symptoms spell FLEA:

items: Fever
Lack of cough
Exudate
Anterior cervical adenopathy

blocks.text: Modified Centor criteria

rows: Empiric antibiotics recommended; consider RADT or culture

blocks.text: Testing. A test is only as good as the sample.

items: Rapid antigen detection test (RADT): 70–90% sensitive, 90–100% specific.
Throat culture: 90–95% sensitive, 95–99% specific.

blocks.text: Treatment

items: First-line: penicillin (Pen G, Pen V or amoxicillin).
Penicillin allergy:
Type IV (delayed) reaction: first-generation cephalosporin.
Type I (immediate) reaction: second- or third-generation cephalosporin with caution, or clindamycin.
Clarithromycin or azithromycin: check local GAS resistance rates first.
Duration: 10 days, except azithromycin (5 days).

blocks.text: GAS complications: rheumatic fever, acute (post-streptococcal) glomerulonephritis, peritonsillar abscess. Periorbital cellulitis is not a GAS pharyngitis complication.
Epiglottitis is inflammation and edema of the epiglottis, classically from H. influenzae type b (Hib); also S. pneumoniae, S. aureus and others. It causes rapidly progressive airway obstruction.
Warning signs

items: Tripod position
Mouth breathing and drooling
Dysphagia
Muffled "hot potato" voice
"Thumb sign" on lateral neck radiograph

blocks.text: Pinch nose tightly for ≥5 minutes. Oxymetazoline Visualization of bleeding Silver nitrate stick Usually: “common cold” viruses Less common: HIV, cytomegalovirus (CMV), Refer if hemodynamic stability, severe (duration >30 min or over a 24-hour period) Nasal compression: Nasal packing Topical decongestant Pharyngitis/Tonsillitis Viral: 50–80% of cases Epstein–Barr virus Bacterial: less common Noninfectious Streptococcal Pharyngitis NOTES
blocks.source: Eye, Ear, Nose and Throat Disorders

blocks.text: The classic tetrad is fever, pharyngitis (sore throat), fatigue and posterior lymphadenopathy. Splenomegaly occurs in about 50%. Diagnosis can be made clinically.
EBV serology

items: Anti-VCA IgM is present from onset to about 6 weeks.
Anti-VCA IgG appears in the acute phase and stays positive for life.
EBNA appears 2–4 months after onset and stays positive for life.
The Monospot test can give false negatives, especially early.

blocks.text: Facial and jaw pain differential: trigeminal neuralgia, TMJ dysfunction, acute rhinosinusitis, dental infection.
Tip: Consider a dental cause whenever a patient presents with facial or jaw pain.
Eustachian tube dysfunction. The eustachian tube equalizes air pressure between the atmosphere and the middle ear.

items: Obstructive symptoms: ear pain, muffled hearing, tinnitus, ear popping, imbalance.
Complications: otitis media with effusion (OME), retracted eardrum, chronic otitis media.
Treatment: treat the underlying cause, such as allergic rhinitis, rhinosinusitis or reflux.

blocks.text: Tympanic membrane conditions

rows: Noninfected fluid from eustachian tube dysfunction. Muffled hearing, fullness, ear pain. Usually self-limited.
May follow OME. Ear pain, hearing loss, pressure, dizziness, bulging TM, often after a URI. Organisms: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis. Amoxicillin first-line.
From barotrauma, a foreign body, or blunt or noise trauma. Sudden ear pain, hearing loss, bloody otorrhea, vertigo, tinnitus. Usually heals on its own.

blocks.text: Name the diagnosis

items: Tragal tenderness and a narrow, inflamed canal: otitis externa
Severe ear pain, otorrhea, hearing loss and mastoid tenderness: mastoiditis
Ear pain, mild hearing loss, bulging TM and a recent URI: acute otitis media

blocks.text: Screening

items: The USPSTF does not recommend universal hearing screening in adults.
The whisper test is useful for screening when the patient isn't aware of a loss.
Refer for audiometry for any complaint of hearing loss. It determines the type (conductive, sensorineural or mixed) and the severity.
In older adults, the most important reason to correct hearing loss is that it leads to understimulation, isolation and possible cognitive decline.

rows: Outer or middle ear; sound can't pass through the canal or TM
Mostly obstruction: cerumen impaction, foreign body (including headphones), otitis externa, OME, eustachian tube dysfunction

Presbycusis (most common): age-related, genetic plus noise exposure, with trouble hearing mid-to-high frequencies, speech distortion, tinnitus. Also acoustic lesions, trauma, ototoxic drugs, noise, hereditary disorders, Ménière disease

blocks.text: Unilateral hearing loss algorithm

items: Start with the Weber test.
Lateralizes to the bad ear: do a Rinne. Bone louder than air means conductive loss.
Lateralizes to the good ear: sensorineural loss.

blocks.text: Ménière disease: episodic vertigo, tinnitus, fluctuating hearing loss and aural fullness. Hearing loss may become permanent. The course is unpredictable, and Dix–Hallpike is for BPPV, not Ménière.
Auditory emergency. Refer to ENT or the ER for hearing loss that is abrupt, unexplained, unilateral and sensorineural.
Lids

items: Chalazion: painless lid swelling over weeks, without drainage or injection.
Hordeolum (stye): painful and acute.

blocks.text: Red eye: major causes (refer)

items: Uveitis or iritis: inflammation from infection, autoimmune disease or trauma
Acute angle-closure glaucoma: rapid rise in IOP
Keratitis: corneal inflammation from infection, injury or contact lenses
Trauma

blocks.text: Red eye: minor causes

items: Conjunctivitis
Blepharitis
Minor foreign body

blocks.text: Red-eye history that needs ophthalmology: change in vision; foreign-body sensation with inability to keep the eye open; photophobia. A scratchy, gritty foreign-body sensation alone is less worrying.

rows: Bilateral mucoid discharge, nasal congestion, sneezing
Sudden severe pain, redness and blurred vision in the right eye
Flashes, floaters, then a "curtain" of peripheral vision loss
Painless bright red pool of blood on the eye after coughing

blocks.text: Glaucoma. Closure of the anterior chamber angle raises IOP and causes optic neuropathy.

rows: Vision loss from optic nerve damage (peripheral first)

blocks.text: Age-related macular degeneration is the leading cause of permanent vision loss in older adults.

items: Dry: gradual vision loss. Wet: rapid, severe vision loss.
Symptoms: central blind spot (scotoma) and curving of straight lines (Amsler grid). Peripheral and color vision stay normal.

blocks.text: Retinopathy is retinal damage from hypertension, diabetes, macular degeneration or genetic factors. Signs: cotton-wool spots, flame hemorrhages, hard exudates, AV nicking.
Eye pain. Refer emergently to the ER or ophthalmology unless noted.

rows: Usually trauma; blood in the anterior chamber
Blood visible at the base of the iris; decreased visual acuity
Foreign-body sensation, can't keep the eye open, defect on fluorescein staining. Specialty referral only if indicated.
Trauma; autoimmune disease such as Crohn disease; infection
Hallmark: pain in the affected eye when light shines in the unaffected eye (consensual photophobia). Blurred vision, possible redness.
Diffusely injected, redder than conjunctivitis; headache; severe pain
Herpes virus; bacteria (Staph, Pseudomonas); overnight contact lens wear
Watery discharge, blurred vision, ciliary flush, dendritic lesions (herpes) on fluorescein or slit-lamp exam

items: Acute sinusitis, epistaxis, pharyngitis and epiglottitis, mono
Hearing assessment; otitis media and externa
Periorbital cellulitis, conjunctivitis, blepharitis
Retinopathy, macular degeneration, eye pain emergencies
For each, know the presentation, diagnosis, differential, management, follow-up, normal course and when to refer.

sections.title: Practice questions (answers in the Answer Key)

blocks.text: Q15.1 Which presentation is most consistent with acute bacterial rhinosinusitis?

items: Symptoms are worst on days 3–6. 2. OTC medications don't give complete relief. 3. Symptoms improve, then suddenly become severe again. 4. Nasal discharge is green and blood-tinged.

blocks.text: Q15.2 A patient reports sneezing, postnasal drip and nasal congestion. Given the most likely diagnosis, what other finding is expected?

items: Purulent nasal discharge 2. Boggy, gray nasal turbinates 3. Petechiae of the posterior pharynx 4. Sinus tenderness on palpation

blocks.text: Q15.3 A 14-year-old with allergic rhinitis and asthma is started on montelukast. The caregiver should watch for serious side effects including:

items: suicidal thoughts. 2. somnolence. 3. headache. 4. anuria.

blocks.text: Q15.4 Which patients with pharyngitis should get a rapid strep test?

items: (a) A 13-year-old with fever, enlarged posterior cervical nodes and tonsillar exudate (Centor score 3)
(b) A 60-year-old daycare worker with tonsillar exudate, temperature 101.2°F and swollen anterior cervical nodes (Centor score 2)
(c) A 25-year-old with cough and temperature 99.4°F (Centor score 0)

blocks.text: Q15.5 The NP suspects group A strep pharyngitis. Which complication is NOT associated with GAS oropharyngeal infection?

items: Periorbital cellulitis 2. Rheumatic fever 3. Acute glomerulonephritis 4. Peritonsillar abscess

blocks.text: Q15.6 A patient with a severe sore throat sits in a tripod position, mouth breathing, with a muffled voice. The NP suspects:

items: viral pharyngitis. 2. bacterial tonsillitis. 3. epiglottitis. 4. peritonsillar abscess.

blocks.text: Q15.7 A college student who has felt ill for 3 days tests positive for infectious mononucleosis. Which symptom is the patient likely to report?

items: Anorexia 2. Sore throat 3. Vomiting 4. Enlarged anterior cervical lymph nodes

blocks.text: Q15.8 A patient has intermittent pain in the left jaw and cheek for a week. Which diagnoses belong in the differential? (Select all that apply.)

items: Trigeminal neuralgia 2. TMJ dysfunction 3. Acute rhinosinusitis 4. Dental infection

blocks.text: Q15.9 What is the primary function of the eustachian tube?

items: Transmitting vibrations to the inner ear 2. Equalizing air pressure 3. Protecting the inner ear from loud noise 4. Producing earwax

blocks.text: Q15.10 What is the most important reason to optimize hearing in an older adult?

items: It affects employment. 2. It reduces independence in daily tasks. 3. People who can't hear can't legally drive. 4. Hearing loss can lead to understimulation, isolation and possible cognitive decline.

blocks.text: Q15.11 Which statement about Ménière disease is true?

items: Dizziness is worse with head movement. 2. The course is persistent and predictable. 3. Dix–Hallpike confirms the diagnosis. 4. Hearing loss may become permanent.

blocks.text: Q15.12 An adult has had painless swelling of the upper eyelid for 4 weeks, with no conjunctival drainage or injection. Which diagnosis fits best?

items: Chalazion 2. Hordeolum 3. Pterygium 4. Pinguecula

sections.title: Role of the primary care provider

items: Tell normal aging from pathologic aging.
Identify the patient's health goals.
Recommend health promotion.
Prevent injury, illness and harm.
Maintain function and community engagement.

blocks.text: Effects of aging on organs: less tissue mass, fewer functional cells, reduced compliance, diminished perfusion and poorly coordinated systemic responses. These changes predispose to disease.
Normal (physiologic) aging follows a predictable pattern, but its rate and extent vary with genetics, lifestyle and environment.

items: Body rhythms change, affecting sleep, stress and digestion.
Dynamic variability (heart rate, temperature) decreases.
Physiologic reserve is reduced.
Presbyopia, presbycusis and mild word-finding difficulty are normal.

blocks.text: Pathologic aging is when normal aging processes speed up enough to cause disease.

items: Example: decreased gut motility and flora lead to anorexia and nutritional deficiency, which weakens the intestinal walls and leads to diverticulosis, constipation and bowel obstruction.
Disease is more debilitating than in younger adults.
Drugs may act differently and cause harm.

Manifestations: dementia, incontinence, dry mouth, atrial fibrillation, infection, ED, tooth decay, hypogonadism, blindness, dehydration, BPH, wounds, fractures, drug toxicity, liver failure, renal failure, burns, falls, constipation, diabetes, pneumonia, anemia, atelectasis, insomnia.

blocks.text: Goals of care are part of the assessment, especially in older adults. Ask what the patient knows about their health, what their goals and values are, and whether diagnosis and treatment should be pursued.

items: The goal is often to relieve suffering, whether the patient's or loved ones', and whether caused by the disease or the treatment.
Suffering is individual: pain, fear, debilitation, death, financial burden, loss of time.
Example: an older patient with Alzheimer dementia and a history of breast cancer presents with fatigue and weight loss. Discuss goals of care before ordering a workup.
Tools: POLST (state-specific), Serious Illness Conversation Guide, Best Case/Worst Case framework.
Advance care planning is billable. Document these conversations and formalize advance directives.
Advance care planning means documenting decisions before an emergency, such as CPR, mechanical ventilation, nutrition and hydration, and comfort care.

Life expectancy covers quantity and quality of life. It often must be estimated for guidelines, especially cancer screening. More disease means shorter life expectancy; life-expectancy tables can help.

blocks.text: Medicare is insurance for U.S. adults over 65.

items: Part A (hospital) and Part B (medical) are the core enrollment.
Patients then choose Part D (drugs) with or without supplemental insurance, or Part C (Medicare Advantage).

blocks.text: Initial Preventive Physical Exam (IPPE, "Welcome to Medicare")

items: Medical, social and family history, focused on risk factors, functional ability, safety and medications.
Exam: vitals, height, weight, and an exam suited to the history.
End-of-life planning.
Preventive services: ECG once, age-appropriate screenings, covered preventive services.
E/M services can be added as needed.

blocks.text: Transitions of care

items: Covers the 30 days after discharge from an inpatient setting to a community residence.
PCP follow-up 7–14 days after discharge.
Medicare reimburses interactive contact and follow-up visits. Pay special attention to vulnerable older adults.

blocks.text: Billable Medicare services

items: IPPE and Annual Wellness Visit
Chronic care management
Nursing home visits
Advance care planning and goals of care
Transitional care management
Obesity counseling
Alcohol and tobacco counseling
Screening for AAA, depression and alcohol use disorder

blocks.text: Tip: Documentation must support a service in order to bill it.
The level of prevention is guided by the goal of care.

rows: Immunizations, exercise, seatbelts, fall prevention, handwashing, dental cleanings, healthy lifestyle (diet, exercise, sleep, community engagement, hobbies, relationships, smoking cessation)
Mammogram, BP measurement, wellness exams, dental radiographs
Smoking cessation in COPD, cardiac rehab after MI, support groups for terminal illness, lowering A1c in diabetes, PT after injury

blocks.text: USPSTF screening for older adults

rows: Per guideline (the manual lists annually; current USPSTF is every 2 years from 40–74)
Colonoscopy, gFOBT, FIT, FIT-DNA, flexible sigmoidoscopy, CT colonography
Ages 45–75; after that, a patient-centered decision

blocks.text: The most common safety concerns are:

items: Accidental injuries: falls; burns from fire or scalding
Poisoning: carbon monoxide, medications, cleaning products
Abuse: interpersonal violence; financial and security scams

blocks.text: Falls. About 3 million older adults are treated in EDs for falls each year, and about 20% of falls cause serious injury such as a fracture or TBI.
Three-question fall screen. A "yes" to any question means increased risk.

items: Do you feel unsteady when standing or walking?
Do you worry about falling?
Have you fallen in the past year? If so, how many times, and were you injured?

blocks.text: Assessing an at-risk patient

items: Gait, strength and balance: Timed Up & Go, 30-Second Chair Stand, 4-Stage Balance Test
Medication review
Home hazards
Orthostatic BP
Visual acuity

blocks.text: Interventions

items: Foot and shoe assessment
Check vitamin D intake and supplement
Look for and optimize comorbidities (e.g., dementia, osteoporosis)
Deprescribe or reduce doses
Relax BP and glucose targets
Compression stockings
Referrals: eye care, OT home evaluation, podiatry, exercise or PT

blocks.text: Fires and burns. Adults 65 and older are twice as likely to die in a fire.

items: High-risk situations: stovetop cooking, smoking at home, electrical faults, space heaters, heating pads and electric blankets.
Consider abuse.
Minor (superficial and partial-thickness) burns can be managed in primary care.

rows: Cool with room-temperature or cool tap water
Clean gently with mild soap 2–3 times a day
Topical agents and dressings 2–3 times a day
Don't unroof bullae; debride if ruptured

blocks.text: About 10% of adults 60 and older experience abuse or neglect.

items: Abuse: physical, sexual, emotional or financial behavior that causes harm, pain, loss or distress.
Neglect: failure to meet an older adult's basic needs.

blocks.text: Risk factors

items: Offender: unrealistic expectations or negative attitude toward caregiving; dependence on the victim for housing or money.
Victim: inconsistent attitude toward the aggressor; dependence on the aggressor for housing, money or care; self-neglect.
Both: physical or mental health problems, substance use disorder, poor stress coping, chronic relationship problems, previous victimization.

blocks.text: Warning signs

items: Neglect: malnutrition or starvation, dehydration, lack of medical care, poor hygiene, undermedication.
Abuse: trauma or fractures in unusual areas, patterned injuries, over- or undermedication, inappropriate restraint.

blocks.text: Interventions: ask patients directly. Report confirmed or suspected abuse to Adult Protective Services or police; this is mandatory. Support caregivers.
Pharmacokinetics (how the drug moves through the body)

rows: Reduced absorption, GI motility, small-bowel surface area and perfusion; reduced first-pass metabolism
Altered bioavailability; standard dose may be too little or too much
Less lean mass and total body water; lower serum protein
Altered distribution of water- and fat-soluble drugs; more free (unbound) drug
Reduced hepatic perfusion and CYP450 function
Reduced renal perfusion, GFR and tubular secretion

blocks.text: Pharmacodynamics (how the body responds)

rows: Stronger effects from opioids, anesthetics, benzodiazepines and sedatives; more tardive dyskinesia with neuroleptics
Orthostatic hypotension; blunted inotropic and chronotropic responses
Less beta-1 response; vascular stiffness; low-renin state
Blunted heart-rate response to beta agonists and blockers; higher SBP; ACE inhibitors may be less effective
Kidneys depend more on prostaglandin vasodilation
NSAIDs cause hyperkalemia and sodium/water retention; TZD-related hyponatremia

blocks.text: Polypharmacy. 22.4% of U.S. adults aged 40–79 take five or more medications. More drugs mean more interactions, adverse effects and errors.
Prescribing principles

items: Start low and go slow.
Prevent prescribing cascades.
When a new symptom appears, ask whether it's a drug side effect or disease progression.
Deprescribe whenever possible.
Don't change several drugs at once.
Avoid potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs).

blocks.text: Beers Criteria (American Geriatrics Society) list potentially inappropriate medications: drugs that raise morbidity or mortality in older adults because of pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic changes. Classes include:

items: Anticholinergics: first-generation antihistamines, antispasmodics, muscle relaxants
Antithrombotics and anticoagulants
Some anti-infectives and some cardiac agents
NSAIDs
Psychiatric drugs: anticonvulsants, antipsychotics, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, TCAs, some SSRIs and SNRIs
Antidiabetics: sliding-scale insulin, sulfonylureas

blocks.text: Prescribing cascade (case of Ms. Biggs). A 76-year-old woman takes Advil PM (ibuprofen plus diphenhydramine) for insomnia. She develops dry eyes (anticholinergic effect) and heartburn (NSAID effect). Her PCP adds famotidine and eye drops. The cascade runs: new condition, new drug, new side effect, another new drug. STOP the cascade by removing the offending drug.

Frailty is reduced physiologic, psychologic and/or social function, often with multiple comorbidities and stressors. It raises the risk of hospitalization, residential care, loss of mobility and death.
Fried physical frailty phenotype. A score of ≥3 means frailty.

items: Unintentional weight loss >10 lb a year (or >5% of body weight)
Self-reported exhaustion
Weak grip strength
Slow walking speed (>6–7 seconds to walk 15 feet)
Low physical activity (reduced energy expenditure)

blocks.text: Frailty interventions

items: Nutrition: low-volume, high-calorie snacks
Fall prevention
Exercise for mobility, gait, strength and bone density
Medication management and deprescribing
Referral for comprehensive geriatric assessment, home health, PT/OT

blocks.text: Insomnia is trouble starting, maintaining or consolidating sleep, or poor sleep quality. It must impair cognition, mood, function or energy, and must not be explained by the environment or another disorder (e.g., sleep apnea).

items: Sleep hygiene for everyone:
Keep a regular schedule for sleep, exercise and meals.
Avoid stimulants, evening fluids and alcohol.
Use the bed for sleep only.
No naps.
Get up if still awake after 20 minutes.
First-line in older adults: CBT for insomnia (CBT-I).

rows: Lowest dose, shortest time. Long-term use is linked to dementia. Beers list (falls, cognitive impairment, lethargy, dependence). Schedule IV.
Best for trouble falling asleep; take only if able to sleep 7–8 hours. No specific geriatric concerns: the safest choice.
Lowest dose, shortest time. Fewer adverse effects than benzodiazepines, but on the Beers list. Schedule IV.
Beers list: anticholinergic effects, sedation, orthostatic hypotension

blocks.text: GFR falls about 50% between ages 50 and 90, with less kidney mass and fewer functional cells.
Renal insufficiency is a pathologic loss of kidney function: eGFR <90, elevated BUN and creatinine, possible proteinuria, abnormal imaging or pathology, and possibly decreased urine output.

items: Chronic causes: uncontrolled diabetes, hypertension, CVD, rheumatologic disease, others.
Acute causes: dehydration, infection, medication toxicity, ischemia, nephrotoxins.
Treatment: assume it's acute until proven otherwise.
Stop offending drugs: nephrotoxins, renally cleared drugs, and drugs that reduce renal blood flow.
Hydrate the patient.
Check for infection.
Control chronic disease.
A single abnormal panel (Cr 1.6, BUN 28, eGFR 34) needs more information to judge chronicity.

blocks.text: CKD means eGFR <60 and/or UACR >30 mg/g for more than 3 months. Creatinine comes from muscle, and muscle mass falls with age, which can make creatinine misleading.
CKD management. At every stage: control underlying disease, reduce CVD risk, cut sodium, prevent AKI, and keep healthy habits and weight.

rows: Reduce sodium; healthy habits and weight
Review medications; diagnose and treat anemia
Review medications; lower protein intake; treat anemia; prepare for dialysis

blocks.text: Depression is common in older adults and adds to disability, medication use, hospitalization and poor quality of life.

items: First step: determine whether the patient meets DSM-5 criteria before diagnosing or treating.

Assess for: suicidality; psychosis and mania; contributing drugs (benzodiazepines, alcohol, opioids); medical conditions (thyroid disease, diabetes, chronic pain, malnutrition); personal and family history of depression.
First-line treatment is psychotherapy.
Expected SSRI effects in older adults: hyponatremia (SIADH), anorexia, parkinsonism/extrapyramidal effects, bleeding, falls. Sinus tachycardia is not expected; SSRIs tend to cause bradycardia.

blocks.text: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop of SBP ≥20 or DBP ≥10 mmHg on standing. It can cause lightheadedness, syncope or angina with position changes. Example: Mrs. Dalton, 69, with heart failure, just started furosemide and has fallen twice getting out of bed. Confirm with orthostatic BP measurement.
How to measure

items: Patient lies down for 5 minutes; measure BP and pulse.
Patient stands for 1 minute; measure again.
Patient stands 2 more minutes; measure again.

blocks.text: Predisposing factors

items: Medications: antihypertensives, vasodilators, nitrates, TCAs, opioids
Alcohol and large meals
Medical disorders: neurodegenerative disease, diabetic neuropathy, autonomic dysfunction

blocks.text: Management

items: Avoid lying flat.
Avoid triggers: alcohol, large meals, heat, high-intensity exercise.
Use physical maneuvers such as leg crossing and squatting.
Increase fluid intake.
Review medications.

blocks.text: About 40% of ambulatory older adults have chronic pain, usually in the hips, back or knees. The goals are to reduce pain intensity and improve function.
Stepwise pain management

items: Nonpharmacologic interventions. Continue them even after adding drugs.
Acetaminophen or topical NSAIDs.
Oral NSAIDs, if there are no contraindications.
Aspirin or tramadol.
Opioids, after a risk–benefit analysis.

blocks.text: NSAID contraindications include uncontrolled HTN, heart failure, reduced GFR, alcohol use disorder and prior stroke. A patient on bisphosphonates for osteoporosis can be a reasonable NSAID candidate.

rows: Any patient with a chronic, progressive disease, regardless of stage, treatment or age (e.g., COPD with breathlessness and anxiety)
Terminal illness with life expectancy <6 months
Quality of life and symptom management; curative treatment can continue
Comfort and quality of life at end of life
Medicare and some private insurers; available in most settings, including nursing facilities

blocks.text: Competence vs. capacity

items: Competence is a legal term for global decision-making ability.
It is presumed until proven otherwise.
It isn't determined by diagnosis or status, and it isn't judged by outcome. Competent people make bad decisions all the time.
It is task-specific, and state laws vary.
Capacity is a medical term for the ability to make decisions about care. It has four components:
Understanding
Appreciation
Reasoning
Communication

The provider's role: check for communication barriers, assess the four components, and use formal tools (Aid to Capacity Evaluation, Hopkins Competency Assessment Test). Do cognitive testing if it helps the decision.
If family question a patient's decision-making, assess the patient to see whether the concerns are valid.
If the patient lacks capacity:
Identify a surrogate decision-maker.
Document the findings in detail.
Don't delay emergent, life-saving treatment.

blocks.text: Advance directive documents

items: Living will: a legal document describing how a person wants to be treated if dying or permanently unable to decide.
Durable power of attorney for health care: names the decision-maker.
DNR: an order about resuscitation.
POLST: portable medical orders.

blocks.text: Erikson stage 8: integrity vs. despair (age >65 to end of life). The person reflects on life with wisdom and fulfillment, or with regret and despair (e.g., "Did I have a meaningful life?"), shaped by past experiences, relationships and meaning.

items: Normal vs. pathologic aging; levels of prevention
Frailty assessment; geriatric syndromes
Geriatric prescribing and the Beers criteria
Abuse and neglect; aging theories
End-of-life and hospice care; advance care planning; functional capacity

sections.title: Practice questions (answers in the Answer Key)

blocks.text: Q16.1 Which represents pathologic aging?

items: Presbyopia 2. Word-finding difficulty 3. Presbycusis 4. Dementia

blocks.text: Q16.2 An older patient with Alzheimer dementia and a history of breast cancer comes in with her daughter for fatigue and unexplained weight loss. The NP worries the cancer has recurred. What is the next step?

items: CT of the chest and pelvis 2. Bilateral mammogram 3. Discuss goals of care with the patient and daughter 4. CBC and CMP

blocks.text: Q16.3 A 71-year-old has an A1c of 8.9%. A medication is added to control glucose and prevent complications. What type of prevention is this?

items: Primary 2. Secondary 3. Tertiary 4. Quaternary

blocks.text: Q16.4 Ms. Finch, 72, has new insomnia. Which medication is the safest choice?

items: Ramelteon 2. Temazepam 3. Zolpidem 4. Trazodone

blocks.text: Q16.5 Labs show Cr 1.6 (high), BUN 28 (high), eGFR 34 (low). Which statement is true?

items: The problem is chronic, from hypertension. 2. The problem is acute, from dehydration. 3. The problem is acute, from medication. 4. More information is needed to judge chronicity.

blocks.text: Q16.6 Mr. Garcia, 69, reports loss of interest in daily activities and feeling sad most of the time. What should be done next?

items: Diagnose depression 2. Start a low-dose SSRI 3. Refer for CBT 4. Determine whether he meets DSM-5 criteria for depression

blocks.text: Q16.7 What is first-line treatment for depression in older adults?

items: SSRIs 2. TCAs 3. Psychotherapy 4. SNRIs

blocks.text: Q16.8 Which side effect would be UNEXPECTED in an older adult taking an SSRI?

items: Hyponatremia 2. Sinus tachycardia 3. Anorexia 4. Parkinsonism

blocks.text: Q16.9 Mrs. Dalton, 69, with heart failure, recently started furosemide and has fallen twice getting up from bed. Which in-office test will confirm the likely cause?

items: Ankle-brachial index 2. Treadmill stress test 3. Tilt-table test 4. Orthostatic BP measurement

blocks.text: Q16.10 Which patient is a good candidate for an NSAID for osteoarthritis pain?

items: 57-year-old man with uncontrolled hypertension 2. 81-year-old woman with heart failure 3. 64-year-old man with a GFR of 47 4. 70-year-old woman with alcohol use disorder 5. 68-year-old man with a history of stroke 6. 60-year-old woman taking a bisphosphonate for osteoporosis

blocks.text: Q16.11 Which new patient would benefit most from a palliative care referral?

sections.title: Scope of practice and exam weight

rows: Preconception care; pregnancy diagnosis; prenatal care up to the third trimester; primary care problems during pregnancy and postpartum
Preconception care; pregnancy diagnosis; referral for prenatal care; primary care problems during pregnancy and postpartum
FNP exam: about 3% of questions (4–6) on pregnancy
AGNP exam: a pregnancy-specific question is unlikely, but a primary care question about a patient who is or could be pregnant is possible

blocks.text: Know your state's scope-of-practice law.

Ginger, ginger ale, saltines Small, cold snacks every 1–2 h Avoid triggers (smells, hot foods) and low blood sugar First-line pharmacology: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) Doxylamine + pyridoxine (Diclegis) Which of the following indicates that persistent nausea and vomiting is likely pregnancy related and not another cause? 1. Onset of symptoms at 5 weeks and persisting to 12 weeks 2. Onset of symptoms after 10 weeks of pregnancy 3. Nausea and vomiting accompanied by fever 4. Nausea with vomiting that is bilious A patient who is 27 weeks pregnant reports constipation. Which of the following is the safest treatment of constipation in pregnancy? 1. Mineral oil 2. Polyethylene glycol 3350 (MiraLax) 3. Psyllium (Metamucil) 4. Castor oil
The purpose is to find and reduce risks to fertility or a healthy pregnancy, and to prevent unplanned pregnancy. Routinely ask women of childbearing age about plans for conception or contraception.
Recommendations

items: Avoid medications and substances that are unsafe in pregnancy. For example, stop ACE inhibitors such as enalapril.
Stabilize chronic conditions.
Optimize diet, activity and weight.
Folic acid 400 mcg daily for average risk.
Consider the partner's health and genetic risks.
Update immunizations. MMR must be given ≥1 month before conception.
Assess the patient's neural tube defect (NTD) risk.

sections.title: Folic acid and neural tube defects

blocks.text: The neural tube develops 26–28 days after conception, often before a pregnancy is recognized.

items: Average risk: 400 mcg (0.4 mg) daily, starting at least 1 month before conception.
High risk: 1,000–4,000 mcg/day for 1–3 months before conception and through the first trimester, then 400 mcg until 6 weeks postpartum. Doses over 1,000 mcg/day should be managed by an obstetrician.

blocks.text: High-risk factors for NTDs

items: Either parent, or a first-degree relative, with an NTD. A second- or third-degree relative raises risk mildly.
Maternal antiseizure medications.
Maternal drugs that reduce folate availability: triamterene, trimethoprim, sulfasalazine.
Maternal conditions that reduce absorption or increase clearance: gastric bypass, IBD.
Preexisting maternal diabetes.

blocks.text: NTDs include spina bifida, anencephaly and encephalocele. Cleft palate is not an NTD.
Symptoms: amenorrhea, nausea, breast changes, fatigue, constipation, food aversions or cravings, mood changes, urinary frequency.
Exam signs (present in the first 4–8 weeks)

items: Goodell sign: softening of the cervix
Chadwick sign: bluish discoloration of the cervix
Hegar sign: compressibility of the cervical isthmus on bimanual exam

blocks.text: Normal physiologic findings include nasal congestion, mild exertional dyspnea and a soft systolic murmur. Increased BP is not expected. BP normally falls in early pregnancy.

rows: Sensitivity varies widely; expensive home tests may beat cheap office tests
Qualitative: rarely needed unless a false negative is suspected. Quantitative: should rise predictably in the first trimester.

blocks.text: Estimated due date (EDD) guides the timing of prenatal care, birth interventions and growth monitoring.

items: Naegele rule: LMP − 3 months + 7 days, plus 1 year.
Gold standard: first-trimester ultrasound, which establishes gestational age.

blocks.text: Pregnancy course: 281–282 days.

items: First trimester: 0 to 13 weeks 6 days
Second trimester: 14 to 27 weeks 6 days
Third trimester: 28 weeks to birth

blocks.text: Diabetes found early in pregnancy. Diagnostic criteria are the same as for nonpregnant adults: fasting glucose, random glucose or A1c. The 3-hour GTT is not used to diagnose preexisting diabetes.
Nausea and vomiting. It is pregnancy-related when it starts around 5–6 weeks and resolves by about 12 weeks. Onset after 10 weeks, fever or bilious vomiting suggest another cause.

items: Nonpharmacologic: ginger, ginger ale, saltines; small cold snacks every 1–2 hours; avoid triggers (smells, hot foods) and low blood sugar.
First-line drugs: pyridoxine (vitamin B6) or doxylamine plus pyridoxine (Diclegis).
Second-line: antihistamines (e.g., diphenhydramine). Avoid ondansetron.

blocks.text: Constipation. The safest treatment is a bulk-forming agent such as psyllium (Metamucil). Avoid mineral oil and castor oil.

items: Avoid fetal drug exposure when possible, especially in the first trimester.
Weigh risks and benefits. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, and refer to OB/GYN if safety is unclear.
Patients should call before starting or stopping any medication.
Pregnancy categories: OTC drugs still use A–X. Prescription categories were eliminated.
2015 FDA Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule (PLLR) sections: pregnancy exposure registry, risk summary, data, clinical considerations.

rows: Folic acid, B6, levothyroxine, many vaccines
Penicillins, cephalosporins, prednisone, insulin, sertraline, triptans, nifedipine; inhaled budesonide (continue asthma controller)
May not be safe (use if benefit outweighs risk, or data incomplete)
Fexofenadine, quinolones, ondansetron, lamotrigine, fluconazole, acetaminophen, GLP-1 agonists, beta-blockers
NSAIDs, opioids, pseudoephedrine, phenytoin, tetracyclines, valproate, SGLT2 inhibitors, thiazide diuretics

blocks.text: Recent warnings

rows: Congenital abnormalities; avoid in the first trimester (ACOG)
Heart defects and cleft palate (FDA warning); risk unclear

blocks.text: Asthma. Continue inhaled budesonide at the same dose. Uncontrolled asthma is a greater risk to the fetus.
Acute cystitis in pregnancy. Treat empirically and adjust to the culture. Fosfomycin is effective and a good choice in the first trimester. Get a test-of-cure culture after treatment.

sections.title: Domestic violence, cramping, weight and activity

blocks.text: Clues to domestic violence

items: Bruising or improbable injuries
Frequent somatic complaints
Depression or anxiety
Late prenatal care (after the first trimester)
Visits cancelled at short notice
An overprotective partner
Consider human trafficking

blocks.text: Cramping is usually normal, from hormones or the growing uterus. Cramping that worsens or comes with bleeding suggests ectopic pregnancy or threatened abortion; most first-trimester ectopics end in miscarriage. Fetal viability is at more than 22–26 weeks.
Weight gain (singleton), by prepregnancy BMI
Maternal weight affects neonatal morbidity and mortality and the child's later risk of diabetes, hypertension and cerebrovascular disease.
Exercise. Continuing an established activity such as running is safe. Avoid contact sports (boxing), fall-risk activities (horseback riding) and overheating (hot yoga).

Screen all pregnant patients for alcohol, tobacco, opioids, methamphetamine and cocaine. No level is safe; these substances are teratogenic at every stage. Counseling is effective. About 1 in 7 pregnant patients report alcohol use and 1 in 20 report binge drinking, most often at ages 18–24.

rows: Placental abruption, fetal demise, growth restriction, preeclampsia, preterm labor, miscarriage, postpartum hemorrhage
Abnormal brain development (ADD, behavior problems), growth restriction
Stillbirth, miscarriage, fetal alcohol syndrome and fetal alcohol effects
Stillbirth, PPROM, low birth weight, placental abruption, doubled preterm-birth risk, sudden unexpected infant death

blocks.text: Opioid use disorder: medication for OUD, including buprenorphine, can be started in pregnancy.
Avoid febrile and contagious illness.

items: Toxoplasmosis: don't clean the cat box; wear gloves when gardening; avoid undercooked or cured meats, soil and unwashed produce.
Others: parvovirus B19 (fifth disease), COVID-19, Zika, influenza, Listeria, CMV, varicella.

blocks.text: Vaccines in every pregnancy, to protect the newborn:

items: Influenza: any time
Tdap: 27–36 weeks
RSV: 32–36 weeks

blocks.text: Avoid live vaccines: MMR and varicella.
Ectopic pregnancy

items: Risk factors: tubal disease or prior tubal surgery, prior cervicitis, smoking.
Onset: 6–8 weeks after LMP.
Signs: unilateral lower abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding or spotting, low-grade fever.
Quantitative hCG fails to double every 24–72 hours.
Example: 6 weeks pregnant with RLQ pain, nausea and spotting. Ectopic is the most concerning diagnosis.

blocks.text: Placenta previa

items: Cause unknown. Often asymptomatic and found on the 18–20 week ultrasound.
Suspect it with painless vaginal bleeding.
DO NOT do a vaginal exam.
Refer to high-risk OB; cesarean delivery is required.

blocks.text: Preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) is membrane rupture before contractions begin, at <37 weeks.

items: Gold standard: pooling of amniotic fluid in the posterior vaginal vault on speculum exam.
Ultrasound: amniotic fluid normal to low-normal.
Other tests: PAMG-1 assay; nitrazine pH; fern test; dye instillation (tampon test). ROM Plus (PP12 + AFP) is no longer recommended.

blocks.text: Preeclampsia is a progressive multisystem condition of pregnancy or postpartum.

items: New hypertension: BP ≥140/90 on two occasions
Proteinuria
End-organ damage, any of:
Platelets <100,000/µL
Creatinine >1.1 mg/dL
Doubled transaminases
Pulmonary edema or heart failure
Stroke
New persistent headache
Visual symptoms (blurred vision, flashing lights)

blocks.text: Preeclampsia management. Refer to OB.

items: Delivery (by 40 weeks or earlier) is the definitive treatment.
Rest in the left lateral position to take pressure off the vena cava.
Balanced diet with moderate protein and sodium.
Antihypertensives: calcium channel blockers, hydralazine.
Hospitalize if BP stays ≥160/110 despite bed rest.
Postpartum blues resolve by about 2 weeks.
Postpartum depression uses the same DSM-5-TR criteria as major depression, with peripartum onset.
Example: at 4 weeks postpartum, a positive PHQ-9 with anhedonia means postpartum depression.

Typical features: anhedonia, lack of interest in the infant, anxiety about caring for the infant, a negative view of the infant's temperament. An increasing need for support and reassurance is less characteristic.
Screen with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale: 10 items, under 5 minutes, easy to score, in 50+ languages.
Consequences: problems with breastfeeding and bonding, harm to child health and development, suicide.
Treatment: psychotherapy, then SSRIs. Sertraline and escitalopram are the safest.

blocks.text: Components: risk assessment, health promotion, education and therapeutic intervention. The goal is to prevent, or promptly recognize and treat, maternal and fetal complications.
Ultrasound indications by trimester

items: First: confirm the due date and fetal development; identify abnormalities.
Second: confirm dates and size; identify abnormalities and bleeding.
Third: confirm size; identify complications, bleeding and fetal position (e.g., breech).

blocks.text: First visit: history

items: Current pregnancy and past OB history
Menstrual and gynecologic history
Medical and surgical history
Family and genetic history
Psychosocial and mental health, with domestic violence screening

blocks.text: First visit: exam. Comprehensive exam with baseline BP, weight and height. Cervical cancer screening follows nonpregnant guidelines.

rows: Urine culture if bacteria present or high pyelonephritis risk
Prevent isoimmunization if Rh incompatibility is possible

blocks.text: Additional first-visit testing

items: TSH if symptomatic or by history. Untreated hypothyroidism can delay neurologic development, and T4 requirements rise in pregnancy.
STI screening (CDC 2021):
Syphilis: all patients in the first trimester
HIV: first and third trimesters
Chlamydia: age <25
Gonorrhea: if high risk, especially age <25
Hepatitis A, B, C: by risk
BV and trichomonas: consider
HSV-2: if high risk or symptomatic

blocks.text: Teach the patient to report: vaginal bleeding, fluid leakage, severe headache, signs of preterm labor, decreased fetal activity, abdominal pain. Also cover weight gain, nutrition, exercise and common pregnancy symptoms.
Visit schedule (uncomplicated pregnancy)

items: Every 4 weeks until 28 weeks
Every 2 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks
Weekly after 36 weeks

blocks.text: Second trimester (14–28 weeks)

items: Quickening at 16–20 weeks.
15–24 weeks: screen for NTDs, genetic disorders and fetal anomalies.
24–28 weeks: screen for gestational diabetes and anemia.
Concerns: RhoGAM indications; preventing preterm labor.
Teaching: reinforce what to report (bleeding, fluid leakage, contractions, decreased movement, preterm labor signs). Start discussing delivery route, breastfeeding, circumcision and car seats.

blocks.text: Fundal height (McDonald rule). Measure in cm from the symphysis pubis to the top of the uterus. From 18–34 weeks, fundal height in cm ≈ gestational age in weeks. Refer if it differs by more than 2 cm.
Integrated (quad) screen

items: Screens for: Down syndrome, trisomy 18 and NTDs.
Higher risk: age >35, insulin-treated diabetes, family history of birth defects.
Markers:
AFP: made by the fetus
Estriol (uE3): made by the fetus and placenta
Beta-hCG: made by the placenta
Inhibin-A: made by the placenta
If abnormal: follow up with ultrasound and/or amniocentesis.

blocks.text: Chromosomal abnormalities

items: Down syndrome: trisomy 21.
Turner syndrome: loss of all or part of an X chromosome in females; short stature, broad ("square") chest.

blocks.text: Gestational diabetes (GDM)

items: Universal screening at ≥24 weeks (24–28 weeks).
Two-step (ACOG-preferred): 1-hour, nonfasting 50-g glucose challenge. If positive, a 3-hour fasting 100-g OGTT.
One-step: fasting 2-hour 75-g OGTT.
3-hour OGTT thresholds. GDM if two or more are met:
Fasting >95
Risks: preeclampsia, hydramnios, macrosomia, fetal organomegaly, maternal and infant birth trauma, perinatal death.
Management: insulin (NPH, aspart, lispro have safety data). Metformin is an ACOG option (not ADA) and is safe throughout pregnancy.

blocks.text: Rh(D) immune globulin (RhoGAM). Rh incompatibility occurs when the mother is Rh-negative and the fetus Rh-positive. Screen at the first visit of every pregnancy.

items: Rh-negative with a positive anti-D antibody screen: don't give RhoGAM. It doesn't work once alloimmunization has occurred.
Rh-negative with a negative anti-D screen: give RhoGAM:
at 28 weeks
after delivery of an Rh-positive newborn
after any event with fetomaternal bleeding (trauma, bleeding, miscarriage, abortion), even if antibody status is unknown

blocks.text: Third trimester (28–40 weeks)

items: 28–36 weeks: fundal height for growth restriction; fetal heart tones and activity; Tdap and RSV; STIs if high risk.
36–41 weeks: fetal presentation (cephalic or not); GBS screen; accelerated growth.
Macrosomia: >4,500 g with diabetes, >5,000 g without.
Routine cervical cancer screening is avoided; cervical checks for dilation and effacement increase.
Postpartum planning: breastfeeding, depression, circumcision.

blocks.text: Kick counts (from 28 weeks). The patient lies on her left side 30 minutes after eating and counts movements. A healthy fetus moves 3–5 times in 1 hour; most move much more.
Group B Streptococcus (GBS, S. agalactiae)

items: Screen at 35–37 weeks with vaginal and rectal swabs.
Causes: asymptomatic bacteriuria, UTI, upper genital tract infection, post-cesarean wound infection, postpartum endometritis, pneumonia, puerperal sepsis.
Complications: pregnancy loss, preterm delivery, stillbirth.

blocks.text: GBS intrapartum prophylaxis. First-line: penicillin G. Alternatives: ampicillin, extended-spectrum penicillins, cephalosporins, vancomycin.

items: Give if:
positive vaginal or rectal GBS screen
a previous infant with early-onset GBS disease
GBS bacteriuria in this pregnancy
unknown status plus intrapartum fever, preterm labor, PPROM or prolonged rupture
Not recommended if:
negative GBS culture within 5 weeks of birth
scheduled cesarean
unknown status, low risk, with a negative rapid NAAT

items: "Your pregnancy will be higher risk because of your age." 2. "It's safe to keep taking enalapril." 3. "We'll have to adjust your asthma regimen before conception." 4. "We need to determine your risk for neural tube defects."
