blocks.text: Use the free CDC Vaccine Schedules app. Don't memorize the schedule; on the exam, make the safe clinical decision.
Live attenuated vaccines are weakened live viruses that must replicate to produce immunity, so they can cause a viral-replication reaction (fever, rash).

items: Examples: MMR, varicella, intranasal influenza, rotavirus, smallpox, yellow fever.
Never give to pregnant or immunocompromised patients.
Give live vaccines on the same day or at least 4 weeks apart; otherwise efficacy drops.

blocks.text: Monitor for 15 minutes after vaccination, because of the risk of syncope.
Spacing. Doses given up to 4 days early are valid. Doses given 5 or more days early are invalid and must be repeated.
Unknown vaccine history. Vaccinate as if the child has never been vaccinated, or draw titers for antibodies to vaccine-preventable illness. Both approaches are acceptable.
Caregiver concerns (CDC advice)

items: Take time to listen; solicit and welcome questions.
Keep the conversation going.
Acknowledge benefits and risks.
Respect the caregiver's authority.
Reduce the stress of shots.

blocks.text: If they still refuse

items: Don't dismiss the family from the practice. Schedule the child and defer the vaccine discussion until a therapeutic relationship is established.
Teach how vaccine-preventable diseases present.
Have them call ahead before bringing an ill child.
Alert other providers that the child is unimmunized.
Have the caregiver sign the CDC refusal-to-vaccinate form.
Resources: 800-CDC-INFO, cdc.gov/vaccines.

blocks.text: Exam tips: establish a connection, speak softly, go slowly, let the child touch the equipment, have the parent hold the child gently, and save the ear exam and anything frightening for last.
Acute otitis media (AOM) is infection of the middle ear.

items: Viral (RSV, influenza) is most common.
Bacterial: S. pneumoniae (40–50%), H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis.
Symptoms vary.
AOM: cloudy, bulging TM with impaired mobility. OME: noninfectious fluid.
A red TM alone, without bulging or immobility, just means inflammation. Crying causes it too.

rows: AOM with severe symptoms: toxic-appearing, pain >48 h, temperature ≥102.2°F
Bilateral AOM without otorrhea, 6 months to 2 years

blocks.text: Refer for recurrent AOM: ≥3 well-documented episodes in 6 months, or 4 in 12 months, despite appropriate antibiotics.
Strawberry tongue (raised red papillae) in an ill child is most often from strep pharyngitis (scarlet fever).
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) usually begins before age 2.

items: Suspect it with: delayed language or communication milestones; regression in social or language skills; an affected sibling; developmental concerns raised by caregivers.
Screen at the 9-, 18-, 24- and 30-month visits, and whenever concerns arise. Use the M-CHAT-R/F (18–30 months), and have a referral source ready.

blocks.text: Bullying risk factors: low self-esteem, being perceived as different or weak, few friends, depression or anxiety.

Eating disorders: children with eating disorders often have comorbid psychiatric conditions. Boys and children of every socioeconomic status are affected, and many patients are not underweight at diagnosis.
Headache

items: Common: more than 90% of school-age children. Most are migraine, tension, cluster or chronic daily headache. Secondary headaches are uncommon. Benign causes include viral illness, stress and eye strain.
History: pattern, burden, family and past history, medications.
Exam: head circumference, growth trajectory, EENT, full neuro exam.
Imaging: MRI preferred (CT if something is developing rapidly) for red flags, an abnormal exam, or underlying disease such as sickle cell or immunodeficiency.

blocks.text: Headache red flags (worry about an intracranial process)

items: Headache that wakes the child, or other signs of raised ICP
Thunderclap onset
Neurologic findings: persistent vomiting, altered mental status, ataxia
Recurrent localized headache or a chronic progressive pattern
Age <6 (history is unreliable)
Personality change
No family history of migraine

blocks.text: Migraine is the most common acute recurrent headache in children. Diagnose by ICHD-3 criteria. It often comes with nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain, and auras are common.

items: Nonpharmacologic: eliminate triggers, reduce stress, rest.
Abortive: simple analgesics, combinations, triptans (age >6).
Prophylactic: cyproheptadine syrup for young children; vitamin B2, melatonin and magnesium are safe and well tolerated.

blocks.text: Seizures

items: Acute symptomatic (provoked) seizure: caused by an acute state such as hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, fever (febrile seizure), toxins, or intracranial inflammation (bleeding, meningitis). It is not epilepsy; treat the cause.
Unprovoked seizure: no provoking condition, or a preexisting brain lesion or progressive neurologic disorder.
Epilepsy: an enduring predisposition to seizures. Either two unprovoked seizures >24 h apart, or one unprovoked seizure with high recurrence risk.
History to take: time and setting; what the child was doing; new medications; systemic symptoms; aura; first sign; duration; loss of alertness; bowel or bladder loss; postictal phase and its length.
A focal seizure with no cause found: order an MRI and refer to neurology.

blocks.text: Lead toxicity masquerades as iron-deficiency anemia.

items: Sources: old house paint dust, water, food, lead pipes, mouthing toys or jewelry.
Symptoms: fatigue, GI upset (stomachache, constipation), irritability, renal changes.
Cognitive and behavioral damage is irreversible.
Young children are more susceptible because of an incomplete blood–brain barrier.

blocks.text: Neonatal bilirubin

items: Peaks: term infants at days 3–4; preterm at days 5–7, with greater toxicity risk.
Breastfeeding exaggerates physiologic jaundice.
Treatment thresholds come from risk charts: bilirubin level vs. age in hours. Escalation of care is based on the bilirubin level.
Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathologic.

blocks.text: Causes of pathologic jaundice

items: Increased production (hemolysis): ABO incompatibility, sepsis, G6PD deficiency, macrosomic infants.
Decreased removal: enzyme defects such as Crigler–Najjar and Gilbert syndromes; maternal or fetal endocrine problems.
Increased enterohepatic circulation: inadequate feeding, breastfeeding, intestinal obstruction.

blocks.text: Treatment thresholds

items: Asymptomatic: use a risk calculator (gestational age, postnatal age, stability). Phototherapy is first-line.

Symptomatic: total bilirubin >25–32 mg/dL. Free bilirubin crosses the blood–brain barrier and causes irreversible bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction (BIND). Escalate care and consider exchange transfusion.

blocks.text: BIND signs

items: Mental status: sleepy but arousable, poor feeding, poor suck, irritability
Tone: persistent hypotonia, or hypertonia
Cry: high-pitched or shrill, hard to console, weak or absent

blocks.text: G6PD deficiency

items: X-linked loss of a protective red cell enzyme. It can cause hemolysis or stay silent for life.
Screen newborns with severe jaundice and anyone with a family history.
Prevalence: Kurdish Jewish 70%, Sardinian 4–35%, Nigerian 22%, Thai 17%, African American 12%.
Acute hemolysis is triggered by oxidative stress:
illness or infection
drugs: fluoroquinolones, nitrofurantoin, phenazopyridine, sulfonylureas
fava beans, henna, naphthalene (mothballs), "poppers"
TMP-SMX is probably safe.

blocks.text: Sickle cell disease (SCD). Sickled RBCs carry oxygen poorly and clump, causing hemolytic anemia and vaso-occlusion: acute and chronic pain and tissue ischemia in every organ system.

items: Functional asplenia makes these children highly susceptible to infection, which can trigger a crisis. Fever can be life-threatening.
Give prophylactic penicillin BID; continue it at well visits.
Ensure good nutrition and hydration.
Live vaccines are NOT contraindicated in SCD. Keep up all immunizations.

blocks.text: Leukemia is cancer of the bone marrow, producing abnormal RBCs, WBCs and/or platelets. It is the most common childhood cancer.

items: Types: ALL 77%, AML 11%.
Ages: 2–8, peak at 4.
Symptoms: anorexia, weight loss, fever, hepatosplenomegaly (>60%), bleeding (50%), persistent bone pain in the long bones (21–38%), lymphadenopathy (50%).
Concerning lymph nodes: enlarged, nontender, firm, rubbery or matted, fixed.
Tests:
CBC with differential: thrombocytopenia in 85%; WBC normal or high, with blasts; anemia.
Peripheral smear: myeloid or lymphoid blasts.
Bone marrow aspirate: blast infiltration.
Pancytopenia (low WBC, RBC and platelets) means bone marrow failure: think leukemia.

blocks.text: Children's airways are tiny, so constriction or obstruction causes big problems.
Pneumonia

items: Viruses are the most common cause in children <5. RSV now has prevention products.
If bacterial: S. pneumoniae (drug-resistant strains common). Over age 5: S. pneumoniae, then M. pneumoniae.
The most sensitive sign in infants is increased respiratory rate.
Chest X-ray: infiltrates. It may be normal early, especially with dehydration. No follow-up film is needed if the child improves.
CBC: bacterial infection shows more segs and bands, WBC >15,000.

blocks.text: Tip: When the poly and lymph percentages are far apart, the infection is likely bacterial.
Treatment

items: First-line: high-dose amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day in divided doses.
Recent antibiotics: amoxicillin/clavulanate or a third-generation cephalosporin.
Penicillin allergy: macrolide or clindamycin.
Avoid doxycycline under age 8 and fluoroquinolones under 18.
Never exceed the adult maximum. For an 11-year-old calculated at 3,680 mg/day, give 1,000 mg TID.
Supportive care: fluids, antipyretics, rest. Hospitalize and give oxygen for respiratory distress.

blocks.text: Respiratory vaccines

rows: PCV 15/20: 4 doses by 18 months. High-risk children >2 years: PCV plus PPSV23
H. influenzae type b: pneumonia, meningitis, epiglottitis
Monoclonal antibody for infants <8 months, and 8–19 months with risk factors; maternal vaccine at 32–36 weeks; adults ≥75, or 60–74 with risk factors

blocks.text: PPSV23 indications include diabetes, chronic heart or lung disease (asthma counts only if treated with high-dose oral steroids), immunocompromise (e.g., leukemia), cochlear implants and CSF leaks. Mild persistent asthma alone is not an indication.
Influenza vaccine

items: Annually for everyone >6 months.
Children <8 years getting their first doses need 2 doses 4 weeks apart.
Egg allergy of any severity: give the routine flu vaccine. No special precautions and no screening are needed.

blocks.text: Bronchiolitis is a self-limited lower respiratory infection, mostly in children <2 years (RSV most common). The diagnosis is clinical.

items: Course: URI for 1–3 days, wheezing peaks on days 3–5, resolution over 2–4 weeks.
Signs: fever (lower with RSV, higher with adenovirus); cough; thick nasal secretions; respiratory distress if severe.
Management is supportive: education, nasal suction, monitoring for dehydration. No bronchodilators and no steroids.
Admit for respiratory distress (nasal flaring, retractions) or poor intake, for fluids, suctioning and oxygen.

blocks.text: Croup (laryngotracheitis)

items: Viral; most common at 6 months to 3 years.
Signs: fever, inspiratory stridor, barking cough, hoarseness, worse at night.
Self-limited, about 3 days.
Steeple sign on AP neck X-ray.
Mild croup: give a single dose of oral dexamethasone.

blocks.text: Asthma is the most common chronic childhood illness and a frequent cause of missed school.

items: History: symptom patterns; triggers (animals, smoke, perfume, seasons, medications); personal or family history of atopy.
Suspect asthma under age 5 with recurrent wheezing (one episode plus symptoms between episodes, or two in 12 months), no likely alternative cause, and improvement with SABA, with or without ICS.
A personal or family history of allergic disease strengthens the diagnosis. Wheezing before age 1 is more likely bronchiolitis.
Treatment differences from adults:
MART with ICS/formoterol is not routine under age 5.
Delivery devices differ.
LTRA (montelukast) carries neuropsychiatric warnings.

rows: SABA prn; short ICS course with acute illness
ICS daily or prn with acute illness
Low-dose ICS daily + SABA prn; consider referral
Medium-dose ICS daily + SABA prn; refer
ICS daily + SABA prn, or ICS + LTRA; consider referral
Low-dose ICS-LABA, medium-dose ICS, or very-low-dose MART

blocks.text: Consider referral at step 3; refer at step 4.

items: ICS and growth: inhaled corticosteroids rarely inhibit growth (at most about 1 cm).
Viral-triggered wheeze in a known asthmatic that improves with a nebulizer: prescribe a 5-day oral steroid burst.

blocks.text: Cystic fibrosis (CF)

items: Autosomal recessive; affects 1 in 2,000–3,000 infants.
Newborn screening in all 50 states; confirm with a sweat chloride test.
Faulty CFTR channels don't export chloride, causing excess salt loss in sweat and thick mucus.
Multisystem: GI tract, lungs, reproductive tract, sweat glands.
Signs:
persistent productive cough
frequent sinus and lower respiratory infections
clubbing, a late sign
pancreatic duct blockage, causing weight loss, greasy stools and dysmotility

blocks.text: Normal heart rate: birth 120–160; age 3, 80–120; age 6, 70–110.
Femoral pulses should be strong and equal to brachial pulses. Weak or delayed femoral pulses suggest coarctation of the aorta.
Blood pressure

items: BP depends on age, sex and height, and rises with BMI.
Start screening at age 3, then annually. Measure at every visit if risk factors are present.
Hypertension: BP ≥95th percentile (or ≥130/80) on 3 separate visits.

blocks.text: Congenital heart disease. Murmurs are common: about 1% of children have CHD and 10% of those are significant. CHD may be found at birth or at 6 weeks or later. "Murmurs are judged by the company they keep."
Murmur grades

items: Grade 1: faintest detectable
Grade 2: soft but readily heard
Grade 3: louder, no thrill
Grade 4: palpable thrill
Grade 5: heard with the stethoscope lightly on the chest
Grade 6: heard with the stethoscope off the chest

rows: Blowing or musical, low and soft
MR to the axilla; AS to the neck

blocks.text: Innocent murmurs

rows: Musical, vibratory, low-pitched; LSB to apex; grade 1–3; loudest supine; no radiation
Soft, blowing systolic ejection murmur at the LUSB; may radiate to the back and axilla
Continuous, whirling; right sternal border and clavicle when upright; disappears when supine

blocks.text: Abnormal heart sounds

items: Fixed split S2: ASD, pulmonic stenosis
S3: ventricular dysfunction
S4: decreased compliance (cardiomyopathy, hypertrophy)
Thrills: VSD, aortic stenosis, PDA
Clicks: aortic or pulmonic stenosis; mid-systolic click in MVP

blocks.text: Pathologic murmurs

rows: Holosystolic, grade 2–3; radiates to the axilla; congenital or rheumatic
Mid-systolic click, enhanced by Valsalva; school age to adolescence

blocks.text: "Bad company" that makes a murmur worrying: chest pain, palpitations, peripheral cyanosis, poor exercise tolerance, excessive fatigue, dyspnea or diaphoresis with exertion (or feeding), venous congestion, syncope or near-syncope.
Pediatric lipid norms

items: Total cholesterol <170
LDL-C <110
HDL-C >45
Triglycerides <75 (age <9) or <90 (ages 10–19)

blocks.text: Dyslipidemia

items: Risk assessment at ages 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, then annually.
Universal screening at 9–11 years, repeated at 17–21, using LDL or non-HDL cholesterol.

blocks.text: Weight categories by BMI percentile (age- and sex-specific charts)

items: Overweight: 85th to <95th percentile
Obesity: ≥95th percentile
Severe obesity: ≥120% of the 95th percentile
Adult BMI cutoffs apply from age 16 in girls and 18 in boys.
A 9-year-old at the 96th percentile has obesity and should be screened for metabolic disease.

blocks.text: Effects of childhood obesity

items: Metabolic: type 2 diabetes, HTN, MASLD
Reproductive: menstrual problems, gynecomastia, precocious puberty
Physical: breathing problems, joint stress, intertrigo, scoliosis
Psychological: less physical activity, disordered eating, bullying

blocks.text: Weight management

items: BP at every visit.
Labs: lipids, A1c, LFTs (if overweight or obese with risk factors), TSH.
Refer children ≥6 to intensive treatment; consider it for younger children.
For severe obesity in adolescents, consider medication and bariatric surgery referral.
Anticipatory guidance: frame healthy eating as disease prevention.

blocks.text: Pediatric diabetes. Type 1 is still most common: 304,000 U.S. children vs. 48,000 with type 2 in 2021. Age at type 1 diagnosis peaks at 4–6 and 10–14.

items: Screen from puberty if risk factors are present.
Symptomatic children: A1c, FPG or 2-hour OGTT, confirmed on another day.

rows: Weight loss, polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, DKA
No antibodies; normal or high insulin and C-peptide
Highest in Black and Hispanic children

blocks.text: Colic: the "rule of 3s"

items: Crying for no apparent reason ≥3 hours a day
≥3 days a week
In an otherwise healthy infant under 3 months
Peaks at about 4–6 weeks. The cause is unknown and it improves with time.
Cultural practices: a flower ankle bracelet for colic is a harmless cultural practice. Respect it as long as it isn't a choking or strangulation hazard.

blocks.text: Pyloric stenosis (infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis)

items: Hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle; 3.5 per 1,000 births; more common in boys.
Classic case: a 2–6-week-old firstborn boy with projectile, nonbilious vomiting right after feeding.
Signs: visible peristaltic waves; an olive-shaped mass in the RUQ at the lateral edge of the rectus, easiest to feel right after vomiting.
Diagnosis: ultrasound.
Refer for laparoscopic pyloromyotomy.

blocks.text: GI vaccines

rows: Start before 15 weeks; no doses after 8 months
Contraindicated with a history of intussusception
Respect minimum intervals; don't restart a lagging series

blocks.text: A newborn of an HBsAg-positive mother needs HepB vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours of birth.
Gastroesophageal reflux (GER)

items: Physiologic GER is normal: up to 30+ times a day in healthy infants.
It becomes pathologic GERD when there is an underlying disease or complications such as esophagitis or failure to thrive.
Red flags:
choking or coughing with feeds
poor weight gain, feeding refusal
constipation or diarrhea, abdominal tenderness
fever
forceful vomiting (pyloric stenosis)
bilious vomiting (obstruction)
blood in stool (intussusception)
Lifestyle measures:
Continue breastfeeding.
Avoid overfeeding; give smaller, more frequent feeds.
Consider a hypoallergenic formula trial; avoid cow's milk and soy formulas.
Thicken bottle feeds with 1 tablespoon of infant cereal per ounce.
Keep the infant upright 20–30 minutes after feeds.
Avoid cigarette smoke, which lowers LES pressure.
Cow's milk protein intolerance: loose stools with blood and mucus.
Medications, for esophagitis, marked irritability, feeding refusal, poor weight gain or failed conservative care:
2-week trial of acid suppression: PPI first-line, H2 blocker second.
If clearly better, continue 3–6 months, then reassess.
GER almost always resolves by 18–24 months.

blocks.text: Intussusception is telescoping of the bowel into itself, causing inflammation and obstruction.

items: It is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children: 80–90% are under 2, with a range of 6–36 months. Usually idiopathic; about 25% may follow a virus.
Classic triad (present in only 15%):
Sudden, intermittent, crampy, progressive pain, often with the legs drawn up
"Currant jelly" stools (bloody mucus)
A tender, palpable sausage-shaped mass
Imaging: KUB to rule out perforation; ultrasound is preferred, showing a "coiled spring" or target sign.
Refer. A stable child may get enema reduction under fluoroscopy. Surgery if unstable, long-standing or perforated.
Rotavirus vaccine is contraindicated after intussusception.

blocks.text: Constipation

items: Normal stool frequency:
Infants: 2–4 a day, decreasing with age; breastfed babies stool more often
Toddlers: about 2 a day
Preschoolers: 1–2 a day
School age: about 1 a day
Recent constipation is <8 weeks; chronic is >8 weeks.
Functional constipation (95% of cases over age 1) needs ≥2 of 6 criteria:
<2 stools a week
Hard or painful stools
Large-diameter stools
A large fecal mass in the rectum
Fecal incontinence
A history of stool retention
Contributors: withholding, dehydration, inactivity, low-fiber diet.
Organic causes:
dietary protein intolerance
neurologic disease (neural tube defect)
endocrine disease (hypothyroidism, diabetes)
Hirschsprung disease
celiac disease
Infant treatment: sorbitol-containing juices or purees; an occasional glycerin suppository. If no response, look for an organic cause.
Child treatment: fiber and fluids; PEG 3350 (MiraLAX) if stools are painful.

blocks.text: Encopresis (DSM-5): a child ≥4 years repeatedly passing stool in inappropriate places, at least once a month for 3 months, voluntarily or not.

items: Constipation underlies about 80%. Withholding leads to a dilated rectum, loss of sensation and urge, and overflow leakage.
Screen for psychological factors.
Management:
initial cleanout, then daily laxative (PEG)
toilet sitting 5–10 minutes, 2–3 times a day after meals
fiber and fluids
a reward system
goal of one soft stool daily; taper slowly over months

blocks.text: Viral gastroenteritis is one of the most common infections in humans: >3 loose stools in 24 hours, vomiting, fever and abdominal pain, lasting under 1–2 weeks. Caused by viruses (rotavirus, norovirus), spread fecal–oral. The best prevention is handwashing (and the rotavirus vaccine).
Dehydration
Tachycardia is the first sign of hypovolemic shock. The best measures of dehydration are weight loss, prolonged capillary refill, poor skin turgor and deep respirations.
Rehydration

items: Mild to moderate: oral rehydration, 50 mL/kg (mild) to 100 mL/kg (moderate) over 4 hours.
Severe: IV.
Resume an age-appropriate diet. Avoid high-fat foods, simple sugars, sports drinks and the BRAT diet.
Avoid antidiarrheals: loperamide risks paralytic ileus. Kaolin-pectin has weak evidence; probiotics have inconsistent evidence.
Refer for diarrhea >7 days, severe dehydration, immunocompromise or failure of oral rehydration.

blocks.text: Pediatric UTI risk factors

items: Boys <1 year, girls <4 years
Uncircumcised boys
Bowel and bladder dysfunction (40% of first UTIs, 80% of recurrent ones): withholding, constipation, incontinence
Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR)
Anatomic abnormalities (uncommon but must be ruled out)

blocks.text: First UTI

items: Treat aggressively, within 72 hours, to prevent pyelonephritis and renal scarring.
Get a UA and culture with sensitivities, and treat empirically with E. coli coverage.

E. coli is about 50% resistant to amoxicillin and ampicillin. Use a second- or third-generation cephalosporin (cefixime, cefdinir, cefuroxime). Cephalexin is acceptable only when renal involvement is unlikely and local resistance is low.
Duration: 3–5 days if afebrile, 10 days if febrile.

blocks.text: Imaging

items: Renal and bladder ultrasound (RBUS):
infants 2–24 months with a first febrile UTI
any age with atypical or recurrent febrile UTIs
family history of renal disease, poor growth or hypertension
Voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) is the test for VUR. Use it if the RBUS is abnormal, the course is unusual, or there is a family history of VUR.

blocks.text: Undescended testes

items: Retractile testes move between the scrotum and above it via the cremasteric reflex. They are normal in older infants up to about 6 years.
Cryptorchidism: the testis may be palpable in the abdomen, inguinal canal or prescrotal area. Most descend by 4 months. It may reflect agenesis or atrophy (e.g., after torsion).
Refer to urology if undescended at 6 months (corrected age), if bilateral and nonpalpable (urgent), or if acquired.
Undescended testes raise testicular cancer risk to about 1 in 1,000–2,500, vs. 1 in 100,000 in the general population.

blocks.text: Hydrocele is peritoneal fluid in the scrotum: a visible cystic mass that transilluminates. It is very common in newborns, and most resolve before 12 months.

items: Communicating: the processus vaginalis stays patent. Size changes during the day and with straining. Assess for inguinal hernia.
Noncommunicating: extra fluid with no connection to the peritoneum. Size doesn't change with crying. Causes include epididymitis, torsion, orchitis and trauma.

blocks.text: Labial adhesions may be associated with irritation or trauma. Asymptomatic adhesions need no treatment (topical estrogen if symptomatic). They can contribute to recurrent UTIs.
An exanthem is a skin rash; an enanthem is a mucous-membrane rash (e.g., Koplik spots).

rows: Fever, malaise, anorexia, then the 3 Cs: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis for 2–4 days; Koplik spots
Within 48 h of Koplik spots: "brick-red" maculopapular rash that starts on the head and neck and spreads down. Order: fever, then Koplik spots, then rash.
Fever, headache, coryza, GI symptoms 2–5 days before the rash
"Slapped cheek" with circumoral pallor, then a lacy macular rash on the trunk and limbs that comes and goes
Minimal; lymphadenopathy and low fever 1–5 days before
Pink pinpoint maculopapules starting on the face and moving down; Forchheimer spots on the soft palate. Causes birth defects and miscarriage in pregnancy.
High fever for 3–7 days, then abrupt defervescence; irritability
Rash appears as the fever breaks: rose-pink macules on the neck and trunk, nonpruritic, lasting 1–3 days. Typical age 6 months to 2 years.
Papules and vesicles on a red base in crops, at different stages; very itchy
Sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue; later desquamates
Oral vesicles and ulcers; vesicles on the hands and feet that crust

blocks.text: Other rashes to know: Rocky Mountain spotted fever, secondary syphilis, ampicillin rash in mono, Kawasaki disease, shingles, Mycoplasma.
Fever plus rash in an unvaccinated child. Have the family call on arrival and wait in the car until a room is ready, to prevent exposures.
Parvovirus in pregnancy. A pregnant caregiver with negative IgM and IgG is not immune and can still be infected. Exposure is most concerning in the first half of pregnancy.

Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) occurs when a shallow acetabulum can't hold the femoral head. It affects about 4 per 1,000 births. Screen at every well visit until 9 months or independent walking.

rows: Barlow: dislocates the hip with posterior pressure
Limited hip abduction at 90° of flexion
Ortolani: reduces the dislocated hip with a "clunk"

blocks.text: Ultrasound is the primary imaging up to 4–6 months. X-rays are limited because the femoral head isn't yet ossified.

Clubfoot (talipes equinovarus) is a foot and ankle deformity present at birth (neurologic, idiopathic or syndromic). It can include equinus (plantar flexion), calcaneus (dorsiflexion), and varus or valgus angulation. Refer to orthopedics for serial casting (Ponseti).
Metatarsus adductus is a kidney-bean-shaped foot from medial deviation of the metatarsals. It usually resolves on its own.

items: Refer if:
still semiflexible at 6 months
rigid at any age
unilateral in-toeing
age >8 with activity limits or cosmetic concerns

blocks.text: Nursemaid's elbow is subluxation of the radial head with annular ligament entrapment, from pulling or twisting the arm, at ages 1–4.

items: Reduction:
Hold the arm extended.
Put your thumb on the radial head.
Apply gentle traction.
Supinate quickly.
Flex the elbow.

blocks.text: Scoliosis

items: Signs: uneven shoulders or hips; one prominent scapula or rib cage; a "hump" on the Adam forward bend test.

The scoliometer measures trunk rotation (not equal to the Cobb angle). Get X-rays if the reading is >7° (BMI <85th percentile) or >5° (BMI ≥85th percentile). Films are standing full-length PA and lateral.
Diagnosis: Cobb angle >10°.
Most concerning: a curve in a younger, still-growing child, such as a 13-year-old girl with 10°.
Red flags for a secondary cause: muscle weakness or other neurologic findings, pain, atypical curve.

blocks.text: Osgood–Schlatter disease (osteochondritis of the tibial tubercle) is an overuse injury in athletes 9–14 after a growth spurt, especially in jumping and pivoting sports.

items: Signs: pain and swelling at the tibial tuberosity, reproduced by extending the knee against resistance.
Lasts 6–18 months, until the growth plate closes.
Management:
continue activity as tolerated
ice
analgesics as needed
a protective pad over the tubercle
PT for quadriceps strength and hamstring flexibility

blocks.text: Pediatric hip pain syndromes

rows: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Hip pain referred to the medial knee, worse with activity, persists at rest; limp; positive Trendelenburg; normal labs
Femoral head slips posteriorly at the growth plate
Weeks to months of pain and limp; knee pain in 25%; limited internal rotation; positive Trendelenburg
Acute limp, often after a URI; no systemic signs; negative Trendelenburg; small effusion
Acute, localized, fever, high WBC, ESR and CRP
Chronic, insidious; rash, uveitis; can bear weight
Hip, thigh or knee pain; normal labs; no systemic signs

items: Trendelenburg test: standing on the affected leg makes the pelvis drop on the opposite side. It is positive in SCFE, Perthes and DDH.
Workup: CBC, CRP and ESR (normal suggests a mechanical cause); blood culture if infection is suspected; Lyme serology; AP and frog-leg X-rays. Refer as needed.

sections.title: Practice questions (answers in the Answer Key)

blocks.text: Q18.1 Considering reduced efficacy, which statement is true?

items: Up to three live vaccines can be given at once. 2. Live vaccines shouldn't be given with inactivated vaccines. 3. Live vaccines should be given the same day or 4 weeks apart. 4. Live vaccines should not be given simultaneously.

blocks.text: Q18.2 How long does the CDC recommend monitoring after vaccinating a child? Why?

items: 15 min 2. 30 min 3. 45 min 4. 60 min

blocks.text: Q18.3 An infant is due for three vaccines at the 4-month visit. The caregiver asks to come at 3½ months. The NP advises:

items: vaccines can be given early if previous doses were tolerated. 2. vaccines can be given up to 14 days early. 3. vaccines can't be given after the recommended age. 4. vaccines given more than 5 days early are not valid doses.

blocks.text: Q18.4 A 4-year-old's caregiver says the child has never been immunized. Per the CDC, how should this be handled?

items: Turn the child away 2. Try to persuade the caregiver 3. Schedule the child and note that vaccines should not be discussed 4. Schedule the child and defer the vaccine discussion until a therapeutic relationship is established

blocks.text: Q18.5 A new 6-year-old patient's caregivers don't know the vaccine history. What should be done?

items: Draw titers 2. Vaccinate as if never vaccinated 3. Either 1 or 2 4. Only 2

blocks.text: Q18.6 A child's TM is red but not bulging or immobile. What does this mean?

items: AOM 2. Erythema indicates inflammation 3. Not clinically significant 4. Allergic reaction

blocks.text: Q18.7 An ill-appearing 8-year-old has raised red papillae on the tongue. What is the most common cause?

items: B12 deficiency 2. Strep pharyngitis 3. Hand, foot and mouth disease 4. Thrush

blocks.text: Q18.8 Which is a possible risk factor for being bullied?

items: Frequent health complaints 2. Low self-esteem 3. Thinks badly of others 4. Easily frustrated

blocks.text: Q18.9 Which statement about eating disorders in children is true?

items: Boys are less likely than girls to have them. 2. Most patients are underweight at diagnosis. 3. Preadolescents with eating disorders are likely to have comorbid psychiatric conditions. 4. Lower-SES patients are less likely to have them.

blocks.text: Q18.10 A 5-year-old has a focal seizure with no cause found. What should be done?

items: Wait for a second seizure 2. Start levetiracetam and refer 3. Order an MRI and refer to neurology 4. Order an EEG to rule out epilepsy

blocks.text: Q18.11 A 2-year-old has microcytic hypochromic anemia with low iron and ferritin. Which statement about lead toxicity is correct?

blocks.text: Well-visit components

items: Interval history: parent concerns, family well-being, family history, social determinants of health.
Developmental domains (by age): personal-social or psychosocial-emotional, language, gross and fine motor, cognitive, moral, physical.
Physical exam: HEENT, lungs, heart, abdomen, skin, GU, neuro, MSK.
Measurements: height, weight, BMI, head circumference.
Anticipatory guidance: age-appropriate screenings, expected growth and development, health behaviors (diet, exercise, sleep), safety.

blocks.text: Age classifications

rows: Born <37 weeks (early term 37–38⁶⁄₇; full term ≥39 weeks)

blocks.text: Assess: gross and fine motor, vision, personal-social, language, reflexes, fontanels.
Motor: lifts the head; equal movement of all extremities; no real fine motor skills. Asymmetric arm movement with clavicular crepitus suggests a clavicle fracture, a risk with macrosomia.
Personal-social: regards faces and tracks the caregiver's eyes, which are bright and shiny.
Language: crying communicates hunger, pain, wanting attention or cold. A high-pitched cry can signal a neurologic disorder (e.g., cri-du-chat).
Reflexes show the maturity of the nervous system.

rows: Moro (startle), stepping, palmar grasp, plantar, rooting, sucking, Galant, tonic neck

blocks.text: An absent Moro (startle) reflex suggests CNS damage.
Head: at birth, head circumference is 1–2 cm larger than chest circumference. Look for molding, caput succedaneum (crosses suture lines) and cephalohematoma (doesn't cross sutures).
Skin findings

items: Milia and neonatal acne
Congenital dermal melanocytosis (formerly "Mongolian spots")
Lanugo

items: The red reflex should be present in both eyes at birth.

Erythromycin ointment prevents gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum.

blocks.text: Fontanels: anterior and posterior are both open at birth.

items: Posterior closes by about 8 weeks (by 2 months).

items: Low-set ears suggest renal agenesis or chromosomal abnormality.

Auditory brainstem response screening at birth; repeat if failed.

AAP "1-3-6": screen by 1 month, diagnose by 3 months, intervene by 6 months.

They then gain about 1 oz/day.

Lungs: wheezing means a workup for exercise-induced bronchospasm.
Abdomen: organomegaly (e.g., splenomegaly in mono).
GU: protective cup, especially after cryptorchidism or with a single testis.

items: Full clearance, with or without follow-up recommendations
Clearance with limitations
Exclusion from participation

sections.title: Practice questions (answers in the Answer Key)

blocks.text: Q19.1 A term newborn moves the left arm asymmetrically and has clavicular crepitus. What might have contributed?

items: Macrosomia 2. Maternal GBS infection 3. A CN VI disorder 4. Maternal vitamin D deficiency

blocks.text: Q19.2 Assessing newborn reflexes is important because it:

items: indicates the maturity of the nervous system. 2. indicates normal muscle tone. 3. rules out neurologic disorders. 4. assesses gestational age.

blocks.text: Q19.3 At birth, the neonate's head is usually:

items: 1–2 cm smaller than the waist. 2. 1–2 cm larger than the chest. 3. the same as the chest. 4. the same as the waist.

blocks.text: Q19.4 A 1-week-old boy has no red reflex in the right eye. This might indicate:

items: pupillary insufficiency. 2. strabismus. 3. congenital cataract. 4. congenital glaucoma.

blocks.text: Q19.5 In a normal term infant, which fontanels are open at birth?

items: Anterior only 2. Posterior only 3. Anterior and posterior 4. Anterior always, posterior sometimes

blocks.text: Q19.6 An infant has no startle reflex (arms extend with a sudden head drop). This may indicate:

items: hearing loss. 2. CNS damage. 3. a visual defect. 4. developmental delay.

blocks.text: Q19.7 An infant weighs 7 lb at birth. What should the infant weigh at 1 year?
Q19.8 A 6-week-old has an open posterior fontanel. What does the NP tell the parents?

items: It stays open until 9–18 months. 2. It should close by 3 months. 3. Refer to neurology. 4. It usually closes by 8 weeks.

blocks.text: Q19.9 An infant just learned to push up on all four limbs. How old is the infant likely to be?

items: 1 month 2. 2 months 3. 4 months 4. 6 months

blocks.text: Q19.10 By what age should eye alignment occur?

items: Within the first 2 months 2. By 3 months 3. By 6 months 4. By 12 months

blocks.text: Q19.11 Which test identifies strabismus?

items: Red reflex 2. Snellen chart 3. Cover–uncover test 4. Visual tracking

blocks.text: Q19.12 A 15-month-old isn't walking independently, rarely responds to their name, and makes only a few sounds such as "ba" or "da." What is most appropriate?

items: Reassure the caregiver that children develop at their own pace 2. Increase social interaction and reassess at 18 months 3. Refer to early intervention for a comprehensive evaluation 4. Order neuroimaging

blocks.text: Q19.13 An 8-year-old caught taking a classmate's toy says, "Because I really wanted it, and no one saw me." Which Kohlberg stage best fits?

items: Preconventional stage 1: obedience and punishment 2. Preconventional stage 2: individualism and exchange (self-interest) 3. Conventional stage 3: good interpersonal relationships 4. Postconventional stage 5: social contract

blocks.text: Objectives: understand the transition from RN to NP; plan certification, licensure and prescribing; recognize scope-of-practice regulation; build a professional portfolio; negotiate employment.
Why certify

items: It shows entry-level knowledge and competence to give safe, quality care.
It assures consumers you meet current standards.
It meets the needs of employers, insurers and the public.
It shows commitment to lifelong learning.
Nearly all states require it for licensure and prescriptive authority.

blocks.text: Study plan

items: Start at least 6 months ahead.
Review course materials and study in a group.
Take a review course and a predictor exam.
Choose your certifying exam.

blocks.text: Applying

items: Apply 2–3 months before you plan to test.

Documents: official transcript; faculty-signed validation of education (completion of the 3 Ps, required clinical hours, practice sites); current RN license; notification of the state board. Use the document checklist.
Tips:
Create an online profile.
Your name must match two forms of ID at the test center.
Choose a notification method and keep a copy of the application.
Authorization to test takes 1–6 weeks.
Eligibility: program completion and graduation within 30 days or already past, with all NP didactic and clinical work complete. DNP candidates can test before graduating.

rows: Multiple choice, drag and drop, hot spot, multiple response
Immediate; official letter in about 1 week
1,000 in the population focus (direct care, administration, education, research)
Plus 1 of 8 categories (academic credit, presentations, EBP, precepting, etc.)
25 non-pharmacology CEs can be replaced by precepting. Or recertify by exam.
Precepting, presenting, authorship, item writing, academic credit

blocks.text: Expired certification

items: Cease and desist: stop using the title and stop practicing.
Notify your board of nursing (BON); it threatens your license and reimbursement.
ANCC: <2 years expired, reactivate by meeting renewal requirements. ≥2 years, complete 75 CE and retest.
AANP: complete the renewal requirements.
Best practice: renew 6 months before expiration.

blocks.text: Staying certified: an active, unencumbered license; online recertification dashboards; renewal handbooks; keep supporting documents such as CE certificates; random audits; notify the BON of recertification.
Scheduling is through Prometric, at a testing center or by live remote proctoring. You are responsible for scheduling and for requesting accommodations.

items: Free cancel or reschedule: 31 or more days before the test, within the authorization window.
30 days to 24 hours before: fee required.
Within 24 hours: no changes allowed.
Hardship extensions to the 120-day window are possible.

blocks.text: Test day

items: Arrive 30 minutes early.
Bring two IDs (one with a photo) with names matching the application. They must be signed; no temporary or expired IDs.
Bring the eligibility letter or authorization to test.
Late or improper ID: you forfeit the fee and need a new registration.
Scratch paper or a dry-erase board is provided; personal items go in a locker.
No scheduled breaks; no misconduct.

blocks.text: Scoring

items: Criterion-referenced with scaled scores: correct answers are converted to a standard scale for fair comparison.
Results are immediate; a detailed report follows, and the certificate arrives in 3–4 weeks.

blocks.text: Retesting. You must reapply, wait, and pay a fee.

items: ANCC: up to 3 times in 12 months.
AANP: 2 times per calendar year.
Some boards require CE first.

blocks.text: State laws differ. You need an active RN license (a compact license counts), fees and documents. Apply through the BON with the checklist: verification of the graduate degree and of certification.
You are "official" when you have an NP license number and it appears on the BON website.
Postnominal order

items: Highest earned degree (PhD, DNP), then non-nursing degrees
Licensure (APRN)
Area of preparation (FNP)
National certification (C, BC)
Awards and honors (FAANP)
Other certifications

blocks.text: Example: Kathy Baldridge, DNP, APRN, FNP-BC, FAANP.

sections.title: Role transition and scope of practice

blocks.text: Bridges' transition model (RN to NP) describes transition as a time of chaos and confusion.

items: Endings: changing identity; uncertainty and insecurity.
Neutral zone: reflection, reinvention, growth.
Beginnings: new relationships; adaptation and adjustment.

blocks.text: Scope of practice is shaped by:

items: education and role (FNP, PMHNP, etc.)
state law (the BON)
continuing education (procedures, specialty certification)
facility policies and procedures (credentialing, contracts)

blocks.text: Collaborative practice agreements depend on state requirements: standard forms, renewal, filing with the state, keeping on site. A CPA is not an employment agreement.
Prescriptive authority exists in all 50 states and DC.

items: It requires a graduate pharmacology course.
Physician involvement varies by state: none, or a collaborative relationship.
Check your BON for off-label rules and restrictions.
You prescribe under a prescribing number.

blocks.text: Federal oversight: CMS (billable services such as diabetic shoes and home health), NCSBN, e-prescribing and EHR rules, DEA.
Professional portfolio

items: Verification of RN license
Transcripts
Course descriptions and numbers, credit hours, years
Detailed syllabi (didactic content, labs, procedures)
Clinical hours log
Capstone or thesis abstract
Articles and projects
CV

blocks.text: NPI (National Provider Identifier) is the first number to apply for.

items: Issued through NPPES, mandated by HIPAA (1996).
A unique individual number used by payers, pharmacies and credentialing bodies.
You need your SSN, date of birth, state license, and practice addresses and phone numbers.
NPI information is public.

blocks.text: State controlled dangerous substance (CDS) license

items: Issued by the Board of Pharmacy; may require BON authority.
Must be obtained before the DEA registration.
One per site, with a fee and yearly renewal.

blocks.text: DEA registration

items: Issued by the DEA (Department of Justice). Requires state licensure and, in some states, a CDS license.
The DEA does not supersede the state CDS.
The DEA number must be on controlled-substance prescriptions.
$888 every 3 years (free for federal employees).
An 8-hour opioid and substance use training requirement.

blocks.text: Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (PDMP) detects overprescribing, diversion and fraud. Every state has one.

CV: heading and profile; education; experience; preceptor sites; presentations; thesis; community service; committees; honors; research and grants; QI work. Keep it updated with licenses and expiration dates, specialty training and memberships, and add it to your portfolio.
Before accepting a job

items: Does the job description match your scope?
Research the practice and its experience with NPs.
Know the expectations.

blocks.text: Employment contract terms

items: Length: 6 months to 3 years; renegotiation.
Compensation: salary or hourly, bonuses, hours, holidays, sick leave, vacation.
Termination: breach by either party, performance, notice period.
Noncompete: how long and what radius.
Performance evaluation: peer review, chart review.
Patient load, on-call duties, support staff.

blocks.text: Negotiation: know your worth. Estimate revenue: patients per day × average E/M reimbursement, projected at start, 6 months and 1 year. Compare to fair market value, which varies by specialty, education and role, and geography.
Negotiable items: CE, memberships, license and prescribing fees, phone and communication, malpractice insurance, professional needs (books, lab coats), promotion of the practice and the NP.
Payment methods

items: Straight salary: a fixed amount for the job description.
Percentage of net receipts: what the NP bills, minus accounts receivable and the NP's share of practice expenses (possibly including physician consultation).
Base salary plus percentage: a guaranteed base plus a share above a set income.
Hourly: paid only for hours worked.

blocks.text: Typical coverage: $1 million per claim / $3 million annual aggregate.
Two policy types (the manual shows these as an image; definitions are standard):

items: Occurrence: covers incidents that happened during the policy period, whenever the claim is filed.
Claims-made: covers claims filed while the policy is active. You need "tail" coverage after leaving.

blocks.text: What it pays for: your defense attorney, lost wages, court costs, licensing board representation. Cost depends on role, setting and state.
Cautions with employer-provided coverage

items: Limits may be too low.
It may not cover lost wages, board hearings or defense costs.
It may not cover volunteer or outside work.
It may not cover suits filed after you leave the job.

blocks.text: National Practitioner Data Bank (NPDB) was established by Congress in 1986. It records adverse actions and malpractice payments. You can submit a statement or dispute a report, and should keep your address current.
Credentialing takes 3–6 months.
Hospital and insurer applications need:

items: state license number
education
prescribing authority
employment history, with gaps explained
NPI, CDS and DEA numbers
procedure logs and training certificates
practice information
standard care agreement
CE log
background check and fingerprints
NPDB query

blocks.text: Medicare: enroll online through PECOS with your NPI and password. Approval takes 45–60 days.

Medicaid is funded jointly by federal and state governments. States decide covered populations, services (e.g., dental, vision), delivery models (fee-for-service vs. managed care) and payment methods. Credential through the state health department's provider relations office.
CAQH (Council for Affordable Quality Healthcare) is a free, universal provider data source that simplifies credentialing.

items: Register after the first insurer issues your provider number.
Re-attest every 120 days.
Documents:
diplomas
employment chronology
three professional references
practice details
NPI
malpractice face sheet and insurer contact
workers' compensation number
licenses
BLS/ACLS dates

blocks.text: Billing

items: Practice within scope and avoid fraudulent billing; productivity drives revenue.
Know incident-to, split/shared, and bundled vs. unbundled billing.
Keep a log of payer billing numbers, hospital applications and procedure logs.
CPT codes (copyrighted by the AMA) describe evaluations, tests and procedures. E/M codes cover visit settings.
ICD-10 codes catalog diagnoses and symptoms. ICD-11 implementation is projected for 2025–2027.
NCSBN (state practice acts)
AANP State Practice Environment map
CMS (reimbursement and HIPAA)
Professional memberships: CE, networking, prestige, leadership, health policy, precepting, PAC contributions.

blocks.text: Key links: NPI at nppes.cms.hhs.gov; CAQH at caqh.org; DEA at deadiversion.usdoj.gov; Medicare at cms.gov. Certifying bodies: AANPCB (aanpcert.org), ANCC (nursingworld.org), AACN, PNCB.
This module has no practice questions.

Procedure logs, certificate of training Practice information: phone and fax numbers, address, contact person Standard care agreement Continuing education hour log Background check & fingerprinting National Practitioner Data Bank inquiry AppENDIX Entry into Practice | Council for Affordable Quality Healthcare (CAQH)
What each exam emphasizes in professional issues

items: AANP: patient and family education and counseling; health care finance, economics and policy; legal and ethical issues; cultural responsiveness; epidemiology, population health and social determinants of health; interprofessional practice; therapeutic communication; transitions of care.

ANCC: ethics and law in health IT; APRN scope and standards; regulatory guidelines; evidence-based guidelines and standards of care; ethical and legal principles for patients, populations and systems; research appraisal; therapeutic communication.

Loretta Ford, EdD, PNP, FAAN, founded the first NP program in 1965 with Dr. Henry Silver, MD, at the University of Colorado. It was a pediatric program, created because physicians were leaving primary care for specialties.
The role met resistance from nurses (over the title) and from other professionals (over practice without physician supervision).

blocks.text: Education timeline

items: 1965: certificate and continuing education
1970s: federal funding for NP programs
1980s–90s: master's programs
2010s–20s: clinical DNP

blocks.text: NP facts

items: More than 400 NP programs and more than 385,000 licensed NPs.
About 39,000 graduates in 2021–2022.
88% are certified in primary care.
Prescriptive authority in all 50 states and DC.

blocks.text: Population focus: FNP 70.3%; AGPC 8.9%; PMHNP 6.5%; AGAC 6.1%; peds primary care 2.4%; women's health 2.2%; peds acute care 0.6%; neonatal 0.5%. Retired exams: adult PC 5.7%, adult AC 2.9%, gerontology 0.9%.
Employment and outlook

items: Settings: 48% physician offices, 22% hospitals, 9% outpatient centers, 4% other practitioner offices.
Bureau of Labor Statistics: NP jobs projected to grow 45% from 2022 to 2032 (118,600 new jobs).

blocks.text: The four APRN roles: NP, CNM, CRNA and CNS. All require a BSN and graduate education. The CNS needs no license beyond the RN in some states.
APRN Consensus Model (2008, with NCSBN) defines an APRN as someone who:

items: completed an accredited graduate program in one of the four roles
passed a national certification exam measuring role and population competencies, and maintains continued competence
has advanced clinical knowledge and skill for direct and indirect care
builds on RN competencies with greater depth, synthesis, complexity and autonomy
is responsible and accountable for health promotion and maintenance: assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation (including prescribing) and evaluation
has clinical experience sufficient for the intended license
is licensed in one of the four roles

blocks.text: Common APRN responsibilities: assessment and diagnosis; treatment planning; direct care; health promotion and disease prevention; research and QI; collaboration; leadership; education; advocacy and policy.
Why the DNP?

items: Advanced competencies for complex practice, faculty and leadership roles.
Better patient outcomes and stronger leadership.
Credits and time that better match the credential.
A practice doctorate for those who don't want a research focus.
Attracts people from non-nursing backgrounds and increases practice faculty.

blocks.text: Five trending APRN roles

items: Developing, using and translating evidence
Relationship building and the human experience
Redesigning care delivery
Innovation and partnerships
Global communication and dissemination

blocks.text: AACN Essentials (2021) set core competencies for entry-level and advanced nursing education: identical competencies with level-specific sub-competencies. They span four spheres of care: disease prevention and health promotion, chronic disease care, regenerative and restorative care, and hospice and palliative care.
The 10 domains

items: Knowledge for nursing practice
Person-centered care
Population health
Scholarship
Quality and safety
Interprofessional partnerships
Systems-based practice
Informatics
Professionalism
Personal, professional and leadership development

blocks.text: Competency-based education (CBE), as AACN defines it, is instruction, assessment, feedback, self-reflection and reporting based on students demonstrating the expected knowledge, attitudes and skills.

items: The adult learner is responsible for mastery and works with clear performance expectations.
The learner reflects, analyzes, judges, resolves, discovers, interacts and creates, and keeps self-reflecting in practice.

blocks.text: NONPF core competencies: leadership; quality; practice inquiry; technology and information literacy; policy; health delivery systems; ethics; independent practice. Plus population-focused competencies.
Scope of practice is the set of services a qualified professional is competent and permitted to perform under their license.
Factors that shape scope

items: Education, training and certification: role and population, national certification, additional training (e.g., joint injections, Nexplanon).
The state Nurse Practice Act, as interpreted by the Board of Nursing.
Facility policies and procedures.

blocks.text: Am I within my scope? Ask four questions:

items: Am I educated (role and population) to do it?
Is it restricted by state law or the BON?
Am I competent and comfortable doing it?
Does the facility allow it?

blocks.text: LACE model of regulation

items: Licensure grants authority to practice.
Accreditation: a recognized agency approves the education program or certification.
Certification recognizes knowledge, skills and achievement of professional standards.
Education: formal graduate or postgraduate certificate preparation.

blocks.text: Prescriptive authority

items: State practice environment: full, reduced or restricted. The BON sets rules on controlled substances, off-label use, weight-loss drugs and CE.
State Board of Pharmacy: compounding, the PDMP, controlled-substance limits.
DEA: national rules; electronic transmission.

blocks.text: Reimbursement authority

items: State licensure establishes scope.
Medicare requires an NPI and permits direct billing. Services must be medically necessary and within scope.
Medicare credentialing requires certification and state licensure.

blocks.text: Scope vs. standards: scope defines the boundaries; standards describe the expected level of care.
Standards of practice keep practice safe and competent:

items: Be a qualified practitioner.
Follow the process of care.
Emphasize priorities: education, shared decision-making, optimal health, continual competence.
Meet interprofessional and collaborative responsibilities.
Document accurately.
Advocate for patients.
Assure quality and continued competence: QA, record review, current EBP, certification, legal compliance.
Fill integral roles: mentor, preceptor, educator, researcher, advocate.
Use research as the basis for practice.

blocks.text: Process of care

items: Assessment: comprehensive history; age-appropriate exam; preventive and diagnostic tests; risk factors; social determinants of health.
Diagnosis: diagnostic reasoning; synthesize data; a prioritized differential.
Plan: tests; priorities for patient, family and community; drug and non-drug orders; education tailored to health literacy; consults and referrals by evidence and shared decision-making.
Implementation: individualized; evidence-based; includes teaching.
Evaluation: is the plan working? Document outcomes; reassess and modify with the patient and family.

blocks.text: Case presentation order

items: CC in the patient's own words
HPI: onset, duration, severity, location, modifying factors
PMH: chronic disease, surgery, injuries
FH: parents, siblings, children, with ages and causes of death
SH: environment, behaviors, marital status, education, diet, smoking
Medications: prescription, OTC, vitamins, herbs
Allergies: drugs, foods, pets, environmental
ROS
Exam: general appearance, head to toe
Diagnostics: abnormal or pertinent results
Differential, ranked by probability, and the working diagnosis
Management of each problem, with rationale, therapeutics and education
Evaluation: follow-up, expected course, referral, complications

blocks.text: Collaboration, consultation and referral

items: Collaboration: joint communication and decision-making.
Consultation: asking for advice on a diagnosis or plan; you keep the patient.
Referral: another provider takes over ongoing treatment of a specific problem.
When to use them: you need advice, the treatment failed, a specialized procedure is needed, the patient asks, or it is beyond your scope.

blocks.text: Interprofessional collaboration (from The Future of Nursing 2020–2030, NASEM 2021) has four core competencies:

items: Values and ethics: respect and trust, toward equitable care.
Roles and responsibilities: know and explain your role and understand others'.
Interprofessional communication: concise and transparent.
Teams and teamwork: effective leadership, better outcomes, fewer errors.

blocks.text: Evidence-based practice (EBP) applies research findings to daily care and decisions.
Five steps

items: Ask a clinical question, using PICO-T: patient or population, intervention, comparison, outcome, time.
Obtain the best literature: search databases with key words and select articles.
Appraise: study design, quality, consistency.
Integrate the evidence with clinical expertise and patient preferences and values.
Evaluate the outcomes.

blocks.text: Clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) are systematically developed, evidence-informed recommendations that weigh risks and benefits. They are not fixed rules. They combine traditional standards of care with research.
How guidelines are developed

items: A detailed literature search.
Construction by a small, representative group.
Testing by professionals not involved in development, for clarity, consistency and acceptability.
Periodic review and revision.

blocks.text: Trustworthy guidelines are:

items: Valid (predictable gains and costs)
Cost-effective
Reproducible (another group would reach the same recommendations)
Reliable (another clinician would apply them the same way)
Representative (all key disciplines, including patients)
Clinically applicable
Flexible (exceptions and patient preferences)
Clear
Meticulously documented, with evidence grades
Reviewed periodically

blocks.text: Guidelines must also be disseminated (journals, targeted mailings, education) and implemented, addressing barriers such as time, cost and staff. Developers should disclose conflicts of interest.
Disagreements between guidelines are usually minor (e.g., screening start age). They come from weak evidence, small samples or differing resources.
Pluralism: the U.S. has many guideline makers, including specialty societies, private groups, AHRQ and USPSTF. The U.K. has a single body, NICE.

The standard of care is the level of care relevant to a specific situation. It decides liability: would a similarly credentialed and experienced provider with the same resources have acted the same way?
To prove negligence (breach), the plaintiff must show all four:

items: Duty: the provider owed a duty of care.
Breach of the standard.
Harm or injury.
Causation: the negligence caused or contributed to the harm.

blocks.text: Examples of breach

items: Failure to diagnose
Misdiagnosis
Lack of follow-up
Misreading labs
Prescription errors (wrong drug, dose or condition)
Intentional harm, which may also be criminal

blocks.text: A breach can occur through error, omission, delay, or inappropriate use of resources.
Common malpractice claims against NPs

items: Practicing outside scope
Improper prescribing of controlled drugs
Failure to monitor (e.g., drug levels)
Incomplete assessment or documentation
Patient rights violations
Confidentiality breaches

blocks.text: Malpractice insurance

items: Typical limits: $1 million per claim, $3 million aggregate.
Claims-made policies need tail coverage after you leave (or "nose" coverage purchased by a new insurer).
Occurrence policies cover any incident during the policy period, whenever it is filed.
Coverage pays for the defense attorney, lost wages, court costs and board representation.
Employer policies may have low limits, may not cover outside or volunteer work or board hearings, and may not cover suits filed after you leave.

blocks.text: National Practitioner Data Bank (NPDB)

items: Created by: Title IV of the Health Care Quality Improvement Act of 1986, with later additions in 1987 and in HIPAA 1996. It is run by HHS/HRSA.
Purpose: improve quality, protect the public, fight fraud and abuse, and stop incompetent providers moving between states.
It collects:
malpractice payments
adverse license, privilege and professional society actions
DEA actions
Medicare and Medicaid exclusions
reports from law enforcement, peer review and health plans
Who can query:
hospitals and health care entities
licensing boards
practitioners about themselves
attorneys, only with proof a hospital failed to query
researchers, de-identified data only
Self-query: keep your address current; you can dispute a report or submit a statement.

blocks.text: Hierarchy of evidence (strongest to weakest)

rows: Combines many studies. A meta-analysis is level 1 only when paired with a systematic review.
Random assignment to control or intervention; controls other factors
Groups with different exposures followed forward for outcomes
Cases matched to controls; looks back (retrospective)
A single patient or a small series
Words, pictures or objects, exploring and describing
Phenomenologic, ethnographic, grounded theory, historical, case study, action research
Interprets the data as it emerges; subjectivity accepted

blocks.text: Qualitative designs

items: Phenomenology: lived experience, through participants' descriptions.
Ethnography: cultural groups in their natural setting.
Grounded theory: constant comparison of data to develop a theory (e.g., why patients miss follow-ups).
Historical: historical data checked for authenticity (external) and accuracy (internal) (e.g., Pearl Harbor).
Action research: investigation plus intervention to solve a problem (e.g., a teacher testing a new reading method).

blocks.text: Applicability is how far results apply to your setting and patient.

items: Organize the factors with PICOS.
Report key characteristics: efficacy vs. effectiveness.
Judge major limitations.
Summarize applicability across the body of evidence.

blocks.text: PICOS questions

items: Population: do my patients match the study's age, ethnicity, SES and problem?
Intervention: how does it compare with routine practice?
Comparison: is the comparator the best alternative?
Outcome: are the most important benefits and harms measured, over a relevant time?
S stands for setting or study type; T for time frame.

blocks.text: GRADE rates the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations transparently.

rows: More research is very unlikely to change confidence. Several high-quality, consistent studies.
More research may change the estimate. One high-quality study, or several with limitations.
More research is likely to change the estimate. Studies with severe limitations.
Any estimate is very uncertain. Expert opinion or no direct evidence.

blocks.text: Strength of recommendation

items: High: the true effect is similar to the estimate.
Moderate: probably close.
Low: might be markedly different.
Very low: probably markedly different.

blocks.text: Certainty goes down with: risk of bias, imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness, publication bias. Certainty goes up with: a very large effect, a dose–response gradient, or residual confounding that would shrink the effect.
Three ethical frameworks

rows: Judge actions only by their consequences
Follow the rules, regardless of consequences
Use the four principles (autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice) plus virtue and practical wisdom
No method for choosing between principles

blocks.text: Core principles

items: Beneficence: act in the patient's best interest.
Autonomy: the patient lives by their own reasons and choices.
Nonmaleficence: do no harm; the patient is no worse off after care.
Justice: distributive justice, with fair and equitable treatment for all.
Fiduciary relationship: the provider acts in the patient's best interest (trust).
Fidelity: keep promises; give competent, safe care.
Paternalism: deciding for a patient without their explicit consent, believing it is in their interest.

blocks.text: Refusing treatment

items: A patient may refuse beneficial treatment (autonomy).
A provider may decline to give a treatment they believe does more harm than good (nonmaleficence). This is situational and regulated by the state.

blocks.text: Informed consent is essential to autonomy, for treatment or research. Discuss and document:

items: the nature of the procedure
its risks and benefits
reasonable alternatives
the risks and benefits of the alternatives
the patient's understanding of 1–4

blocks.text: Also document the patient's participation, avoid coercion, and give your recommendation and reasoning.
Three legal standards for disclosure

items: Subjective: what does this patient need to know?
Reasonable patient: what would an average patient need to know? This is the most commonly used standard.
Reasonable provider: what would a typical provider disclose?

blocks.text: Exceptions to informed consent

items: Incapacity. Proof may be needed. Without a designated decision-maker, follow the state hierarchy of surrogates; if that fails, a court appoints a guardian.
Life-threatening emergency with no time to get consent.
Voluntary waiver by the patient.

blocks.text: Minors (unemancipated) can't consent; get informed permission from a parent or guardian. Emancipated minors include those who are married, in the military, financially independent, or parents themselves. Check state law.
Research ethics. IRBs were established by the National Research Act of 1974, after the Tuskegee syphilis study.

items: Valid research consent requires disclosure, competency and voluntariness.
Consent can be waived for minimal-risk studies (e.g., retrospective chart reviews).

blocks.text: Shared decision-making (SDM) is a form of informed consent, used when more than one reasonable option exists. It helps reduce disparities.

items: It requires:
unbiased evidence on the options, including no intervention
clinician skill in communicating and tailoring that evidence
the patient's goals, preferences and concerns, including treatment burden
AHRQ SHARE steps:
Seek participation.
Help explore and compare options.
Assess values and preferences.
Reach a decision.
Evaluate the decision.

blocks.text: EMTALA (42 U.S.C. §1395dd, part of COBRA) comes from beneficence and justice. Hospitals must screen and stabilize emergency patients regardless of ability to pay. Problems arise in deciding what counts as an emergency and when a patient is stable.
Confidentiality and HIPAA. Confidentiality comes from the fiduciary relationship and from autonomy: the patient controls who knows their health status.

items: Exceptions: imminent danger to the patient or others; certain infectious diseases; reportable STIs.

items: Autonomy: the patient controls who sees their information.

Beneficence: chart accurate facts.

items: Copy-and-paste (content importing) from other providers, other patients or prior visits causes inaccuracy and legal liability.
Incomplete structured data.
Decision-support tools (diagnosis aids, drug recommendations, calculators) don't replace critical thinking.
Unanswered liability questions: a faulty EHR recommendation; a vendor's responsibility; a misleading display; ignoring alerts without documenting your reasoning.

items: Short auto-logout

items: Teach patients about online information and unreliable sites, and caution them about buying prescriptions online.
Never post photos or PHI on social media, even if the patient isn't identifiable.
Don't complain online about patients or colleagues.
Don't require patients to sign a no-negative-review pledge. It is coercive.

blocks.text: Epidemiology studies how often disease occurs in groups and why. It describes the disease burden, finds causes and determinants, tests interventions, informs policy and evaluates programs. Its conclusions about a population at risk come from comparisons (etiology, risk factors, morbidity and mortality).

rows: Spread over a larger area or many countries

blocks.text: Healthy People 2030 (Office of Disease Prevention and Health Promotion) sets national goals over 10 years:

items: Long, high-quality lives free of preventable disease, disability, injury and early death.
Health equity and the elimination of disparities.
Social and physical environments that support health.
Healthy development and behaviors at every life stage.

blocks.text: Its principles are health equity, shared responsibility, data-driven objectives, and attention to social, physical and economic environments. It draws on EBP, epidemiology and the levels of prevention.
Notifiable diseases

items: Nationally notifiable to CDC. Waterborne: cholera, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Giardia, hepatitis A, Legionella, malaria, Salmonella, Shigella, typhoid, Vibrio, yellow fever. Others: cancer, chancroid, chlamydia, COVID-19, gonorrhea, HIV, influenza-associated pediatric deaths, Lyme, mumps, pertussis and more.
State-reportable lists exist in every state. Reporting is the provider's responsibility.
Written report: e.g., gonorrhea, salmonellosis.
Telephone report: e.g., measles, pertussis.
Total case counts: e.g., chickenpox, influenza.
Cancer goes to the state cancer registry.

blocks.text: Abuse reporting. Laws are state-specific.

items: Mandatory reporters: health care providers, childcare workers, clergy, coaches and educators, counselors, law enforcement.
Covered populations: children (federal CAPTA), people with disabilities, older adults; intimate partners vary by state.
Types: physical, sexual, emotional, financial.
Scale: 1 in 8 children are affected, and homicide is a top-5 cause of child death. Intimate partner violence affects about 1 in 3 women and 17% of men. About 10% of adults ≥60 experience abuse.
Mandatory reporters must report suspicion. The burden of proof is NOT on the reporter.

blocks.text: ANA Standard 8: culturally congruent practice. "Health care isn't one-size-fits-all." Use shared decision-making that respects cultural norms, even when they may conflict with EBP, and identify the patient's cultural and language needs.

Culture is learned, shared knowledge that groups use to guide behavior and interpret the world: beliefs, interaction norms, morals, customs, technologies and survival strategies. It shapes work, parenting, marriage, and understanding of health, illness, disability and death.
Four components of culturally congruent care

items: Cultural diversity: age, gender, sexual orientation, SES, education, race, ethnicity, language, religion; differences between and within groups.
Cultural awareness (cognitive): understand what culture is, intracultural variation, and your own biases; reflect on your reactions.
Cultural responsiveness (affective): openness; no right or wrong values on differences.
Cultural competence (behavioral): a dynamic process of gaining knowledge and skills and adapting care.

blocks.text: Assimilation vs. acculturation

items: Assimilation: one culture fully absorbs the other.
Acculturation: a group adopts some practices of the host culture but keeps identifiable differences.

blocks.text: Anticipatory guidance is education and proactive counseling that complements risk assessment: risk reduction, health promotion, disease prevention, complications. Use it for:

items: pediatric development
risk reduction at every age
disease progression
crises
major life changes
end of life

blocks.text: End-of-life guidance

items: Advance care planning: goals, values and preferences; timelines; living will and durable power of attorney; organ donation; POLST/MOLST.
After-death wishes: will or trust, finances, funeral plans.
Palliative care: begins at diagnosis of a serious illness; disease treatment continues; the PCP stays involved; addresses symptoms and emotional, social, practical and spiritual needs.
Treatment discontinuation: when burdens outweigh benefits and goals shift from cure to comfort.
Hospice: comfort at the end of life, at home, in hospital or in a nursing home, after curative treatment stops; teaches caregivers what to expect.

blocks.text: Levels of influence on health behavior (education works best when it targets several levels)

items: Intrapersonal: knowledge, attitudes, beliefs, personality.
Interpersonal: family, friends and peers.
Institutional: rules, policies and structures.
Community: social networks and norms.
Public policy: local, state and federal laws.

blocks.text: Health Belief Model. The manual shows it as an image; the constructs are standard. People act when they perceive susceptibility and severity, see benefits that outweigh barriers, encounter cues to action, and have self-efficacy.

rows: Educate; personalize the risks and benefits
Aware of the problem and intends to act, but not committed

blocks.text: Theory of planned behavior: behavioral intention is driven by attitude (is the behavior good or bad?), subjective norm (do key people approve?) and perceived behavioral control (is it up to me?).
Motivational interviewing (MI) is a guiding style between following and directing. It draws out the patient's own reasons for change, collaborates, and honors autonomy.

items: Spirit:
Partnership: the patient is the expert on their life.

Open questions

Summarizing

Planning: an acceptable, accessible change plan.

blocks.text: Family systems theory (Murray Bowen) sees the family as an interconnected emotional unit with reciprocal relationships. Its 8 concepts:

Differentiation of self

Family projection process
Multigenerational transmission

Emotional process in society

blocks.text: Family assessment tools

items: Genogram: at least three generations, with ages, sex, medical, genetic, behavioral and social information. Look for red flags such as suicide, alcohol use and depression.
Ecomap: a picture of the family's ties to outside systems (school, work, worship, health care, recreation) and the strength of those ties.
Pedigree: symbols for affected or unaffected, alive or deceased.

blocks.text: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs)

items: Types: emotional, physical or sexual abuse; violence against a parent; household substance use; household mental illness or suicidality; an incarcerated household member.
Stress: positive, tolerable or toxic. ACEs rarely occur alone; 1 in 8 children have ≥4.
ACE pyramid: ACEs disrupt neurodevelopment, leading to social, emotional and cognitive impairment, health-risk behaviors, disease and disability, and early death.

blocks.text: Theories of aging

items: Biologic: wear and tear; immunity; programmed longevity.
Sociologic: roles and relationships; disengagement; continuity; age stratification (cohorts such as baby boomers).
Psychologic: Erikson's integrity vs. despair; Maslow; Jung's individualism.
Moral or spiritual: how a person explains and validates their existence.

blocks.text: Access to care is "the timely use of personal health services to achieve the best health outcomes" (IOM, 1993). Healthy People 2030 names four components:

A usual source of care brings recommended screening

SDOH (income, geography, language, literacy); no choice of provider; transportation; signature authority delays; home health and telehealth barriers
Health Professional Shortage Areas (primary, mental, specialty care); Medically Underserved Areas; safety-net strain
